subsubtopic: REQUEST HOUSE COMMITTEE INVESTIGATE ALLEGATIONS OF DR. CELOVSKY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
In today's Ottawa Citizen, Frank Howard, under the byline "Bureaucrats," publishes a letter dated November 6, 1979, written by Boris Celovsky, assistant director, labour division, Statistics Canada. In this letter, Dr. Celovsky makes serious allegations about the integrity and the reliability of Statistics Canada's information to the government and the Canadian public.
Considering that in Dr. Celovsky's own words, "Statistics Canada's performance record over the past few years has become rather spotty," and that, further, "the bureau has wasted and continues to waste public money on projects which were badly designed and should never have been launched", and considering the accusation by Dr. Celovsky that the labour income, one of the largest components of the national account, is said to have been adjusted, cooked or fudged without consistent technical basis, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier):
That the government make an immediate statement concerning the serious allegations of Dr. Celovsky and that this disturbing matter be referred to the appropriate standing committee for immediate investigation prior to the tabling by the Minister of Finance of his overdue budget.

subsubtopic: RECORD DEFICIT IN AUTOMOTIVE PARTS-REQUEST AUTO PACT BE DISCUSSED WITH U.S. PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I direct my question to the Prime Minister. Figures that came into my possession today, which are widely known, would indicate that we will have a record deficit in automotive parts trade with the United States to the tune of $2,220 million for the first nine months of this year. I indicate to the Prime Minister that this is the highest deficit ever experienced. Also, the projection is that it will be $3.1 billion by the end of this year. This is a 400 per cent increase over the previous year.
Could the Prime Minister indicate to the House just what stress he will put on this intolerable situation in speaking with the President tomorrow, and what action will he ask of the President in order to correct this situation?

He may recall that in 1971, when treasury secretary Connally was in this country, Canada was experiencing a small surplus. In 1970 it was $204 million, in 1971 it was $198 million, and in 1972 it was $44 million. This is a pittance compared to the type of deficit we are now running with the United States.
At that time, treasury secretary Connally said the situation was intolerable from the point of view of the United States and that the United States would be taking unilateral action to correct the situation no matter what Canada thought. Since our deficit is now so horrendously high, is the minister prepared to indicate a strong stand on the part of the Canadian government to President Carter tomorrow?

AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-FAIR SHARE FOR CANADA OF CAPITAL INVESTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. I hope he can be induced to answer a question on the automotive industry. Recently, General Motors of Canada announced a $1 billion expansion program at its parts plants in Windsor and St. Catharines, along with another $1 billion for updating other facilities. Privilege-Mr. Kaplan

MR. KAPLAN-REASON FOR NON-ATTENDANCE AT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege arises out of the answer which the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport and Multiculturalism (Mr. Paproski) gave to a question that 1 just asked, suggesting that somehow or other I was derelict in my duty by not attending this morning at a meeting of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration. I am familiar with the answers of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey), and that is partly the reason why I did not attend that meeting. I know the minister's views on the subject because they are stated in the report, and that is that, as far as he is concerned, the proportion of immigrants admitted by economic criteria should be increased and, therefore, that the proportion of family assisted immigrants should be decreased.
There is a second reason I did not attend that meeting, and that is that it had been agreed in the steering committee not to deal with immigration questions this morning, but rather to deal with questions arising under the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I knew perfectly well that his official on immigration would not be there and it would be a breach of agreement among the members of the committee to pursue the matter there.
I was interested in knowing how the minister of state responsible for multiculturalism felt about the matter, because that portfolio has a tradition of-and it is the minister's responsibility-standing up for family reunification, which is of so much concern. I did not know whether the minister had heard of this report on 1980 immigration levels. Obviously, the minister had been overruled if he had made any representation. I wanted to know whether he had made any representation, whether he accepted the report and what he was doing about it. The mandate for multiculturalism should lead the minister into virtually every other portfolio of the government.

The principle of family reunification will continue to govern the admission of close family members-

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should appreciate the President of the Privy Council giving us an idea of the business planned for the House today, tomorrow and next week.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps the time has come in this session of Parliament to go beyond this week and next week. I should like to take this occasion to indicate what we feel ought to be determined and dealt with and finished by this House, and in some cases by Parliament, by the time we normally adjourn for Christmas.
November 8, 1979

First, let me say that there has been some confusion. Various members on all sides of the House have expressed confusion about what we might be doing on Monday. I want to make it clear that the House will be sitting on Monday, November 12. I do that to clear up the matter in the minds of some hon. members who have spoken to me about it.
We will require royal assent by Christmas for the following bills: first, the appropriation bill related to interim supply; the appropriation bill for the main estimates; Bill C-17, the income tax amendments; Bill C-18, the customs tariff amendments and Bill C-10, the borrowing authority bill which I understand is out of committee now and can come back to the House. All of these are really housekeeping matters in terms of the operation of the government and of this Parliament.
With respect to other legislation for which royal assent is required by the Christmas adjournment, there is Bill C-20, the property tax credit bill, standing in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie).
An hon. Mfember: No way.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Forget it.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: We stay here.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
1 do not want to enter into an altercation with respect to that but I want to point out to members that if that bill does not pass by Christmas there is no way home owners in Canada will receive the benefit of it when they file their income tax returns in 1980 for the year 1979.
The other bill for which we require royal assent by the Christmas adjournment is Bill C-6, the old age security amendments and spouses' allowance bill. There is also Bill C-14, the Bank Act. The reason I put that on the list is that it has had an extensive hearing as a reference in the last Parliament and amendments to the bill basically reflect the work of the House of Commons.
There is a bill in the name of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. McKinnon) with respect to veterans' pensions which we will be putting down very quickly. We require royal assent for that bill before we adjourn for Christmas as well. It is a very short list, really.
With respect to other bills, we will require and ask the House to complete second reading debate on Bill C-15, which is the freedom of information legislation, so that the committee can begin studying it. We will ask that the Municipal Grants Act, Bill C-3, be completed at least through second reading and into committee so that it can be dealt with after we come back.
It is my intention to table in the House in a relatively short time-and I will consult with my friends as to when that can be done-a position paper with respect to parliamentary reform. I would hope we would have moved the reference on parliamentary reform, so that the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization can get at the job that has been hanging around for a long, long time and examine how this
Business of the House
Parliament operates and review it in terms of the views of hon. members and the views that will be expressed by the government in that paper.
There is a matter of law that must be dealt with by Monday.
It is my intention to call on Monday, unless other factors intervene, the redistribution reference standing on the order paper in my name. I am required to bring that forward to Parliament and I intend to do so.
That is basically what I would call the particular legislative package for Christmas. If there is time, and I hope there will be-I should like to have my friends discuss that with me because I recognize there might not be time-we hope to call and have dealt with motions standing in the names of various ministers of the House with respect to the four select committees dealing with rehabilitation, the cost overruns, the reference of which is standing on the order paper, and have a parliamentary review of that matter. Then there is the parliamentary review of the Foreign Investment Review Act and its operation, and voluntarism. That is for the purpose of establishing committees and getting Parliament working on those subjects. There is also the question of establishing a joint committee of the House and Senate on the question of nuclear energy. We should like to have that reference made as well, if there is time to do it.
There is one other matter which is basically dealing with the procedure of the House in which I know Your Honour has an interest as you chaired the committee in the last Parliament, and that is with respect to televising the proceedings of the committees of the House of Commons. I hope we can set that up prior to Christmas.
I think it appropriate to give as broad a picture of the expectations of the government as I can for that period of time. However, with respect to the four select committees that I dealt with, the joint committee on the nuclear inquiry and the committee on televising the proceedings in House of Commons committees, I am suggesting these to my colleagues so that they may come back to me to see if we can take those before Christmas. The other items I mentioned and the stages I mentioned are essential to the government prior to the Christmas adjournment.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that we on this side of the House are ready to co-operate. I did not ask the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) to read the order paper at length. What we want to know is what is going to happen in the near future in the House. I asked the President of the Privy Council to indicate to us what we are going to do today, tomorrow and next week. As for the long list of bills which he has given us, for some there is no complication, but for others the members on this side at least would like to take part in a more thorough discussion. But 1 feel it is expecting a great deal from Her Majesty to be seeking assent for the 12-odd bills mentioned by the minister. He is dreaming of a white Christmas. However, I would like to know what we are going to do today, tomorrow and next week. And I would

November 8, 1979
Business of the House
rather not have to ask the question every evening so that on this side of the House we could get ready to speak intelligently and thus closely co-operate with the government to pass legislation as quickly as possible. It would be quite useful to know where we stand in the short term.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT

Mr. Speaker, there have been consultations among House leaders and representatives of the House leaders with respect to that matter. There is a motion to concur in the estimates and a bill will come out of that. We want to deal with that today. Of course, we will only be sitting until one o'clock tomorrow because of the visit of the President of the United States.
On Monday, as I indicated, all things being equal, and assuming we can make progress on the motion to concur and the bill that will follow it today-in other words, to advance the two stages-on Monday I would be calling the redistribution motion. If we cannot make that kind of progress I may have to reconsider, but I would not do anything without informing my hon. friend. That would get us into next week. I think the next priority is to complete the borrowing authority bill, which would bring us to the first part of the week. Beyond that, I will consult with my friends.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
I would like to ask one last question, Mr. Speaker. The President of the Privy Council says that today he intends to move the motion for concurrence in the supplementary estimates and the motion to concur in interim supply and then to introduce a bill. Naturally, the consent of the House will be needed for second reading of that bill so that we may sit in Committee of the Whole. We are prepared to go along with all these things, Mr. Speaker, in order to speed up the business of the House and in a spirit of co-operation with the government. However, I want to bring to the attention of the President of the Privy Council who referred to the last three meetings between the House leaders that in each instance he was warned to avoid including in the motion to concur in interim supply an item which would put us in a position where we would have to concur in twelve-twelfths of the interim supply.
For all practical purposes, if we are asked to approve twelve-twelfths of interim supply, it is a matter of principle; we are being asked to approve the total amount of the estimates. So, Mr. Speaker, I note that in paragraph (b) of motion No. 5, we are asked to grant an additional three-twelfths of the total amount of Energy, Mines and Resources votes 15 and L75. That would add up to twelve-twelfths. It seems to me that goes against what we told the President of the Privy Council and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Baker). That might lead us to move an amendment that might mean a non-confidence motion against the government which might require a vote very soon if it were to take place on second reading.
[Mr. Pinard.)
I do not intend to move that amendment on second reading, precisely not to embarrass the government and so that things will go more quickly. However, in Committee of the Whole I want to warn the President of the Privy Council and Minister of National Revenue that if he does not amend that motion or if the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) does not agree to reduce paragraph (b) of motion No. 5 to two-twelfths rather then three-twelfths, in Committee of the Whole, we will be forced to move a motion to amend in accordance the bill that will follow shortly. I draw this to the attention of the President of the Privy Council and Minister of National Revenue immediately. If he wants open co-operation, let him respect the will that was conveyed to him on three occasions at meetings of the House leaders and not include in his motion items that will result in twelve-twelfths of interim supply being approved. And I warn him immediately of our intention to move an amendment, not on second reading, but in Committee of the Whole.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
The government House leader has done two things. He has given us an overview of what he wants between now and Christmas, and he has indicated what he has in mind for the next few days.
With respect to the many matters on which he would like action between now and Christmas, may I point out that in the case of those four select committees on voluntarism, the Foreign Investment Review Act, the cost overruns and the handicapped, I indicated to him that in so far as our party is concerned we would be prepared to make arrangements to deal with the four of them in one day's debate. If he wants those committees to get going, and I believe he does, I hope that he will consider that offer.
With regard to the freedom of information legislation, I know that the government House leader expressed the hope that this could be done with a minimum of debate. There was even some suggestion of one speaker per party. We have a number of members who wish to take part, but we would agree to a debate of not more than two days at second reading of that bill. I am trying to make suggestions that might help him to draw up a schedule.
The minister has mentioned certain bills that he feels should be through before Christmas. 1 realize that it is important to get on with the Bank Act so that we do not run into extending the ten years into 11 or 12 years, but I believe that Parliament does have until March to get that legislation through. Nevertheless, as I say, we recognize that that bill is important.
When the minister was pleading for the legislation regarding the property tax credit to be put through before Christmas, I was thinking that the minister is not only the government House leader but also the Minister of National Revenue. I wonder if this means he has already ordered the printing of the income tax forms as though that legislation had been passed. That, of course, is a bit risky.
Generally speaking, we appreciate the concern about these bills and we shall do our part. As I say, as opposed to some
Business of the House
things that we may want to debate at length, I have indicated four resolutions regarding committees and one bill concerning which we think action could be taken fairly early.
As to the debate today, and Monday if it is carried on, my understanding is that first of all we will be debating the motions that are on the order paper in the name of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens), and that for those debates Mr. Speaker will be in the chair. It is only after those motions have been passed that a bill is to be introduced.
I understand it is to be one bill incorporating both supplementary estimates and interim supply. If at that point it is necessary to give consent to move from first reading to second reading, we will give that consent. But as I say, first of all, we protect our right to discuss these motions at the motion stage.
At that point we can go further into the very serious point raised by the hon. member for Drummond (Mr. Pinard). I certainly do not recall, and I have been around here for a while, interim supply ever being given for a full twelve-twelfths. Yet simple arithmetic tells me that nine-twelfths plus three-twelfths is twelve-twelfths.

Mr. Speaker, I rise as a member who for only a few months has watched some of the members of the Liberal party asking questions. 1 believe the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) should be paid heed to when he states that when they take up a lot of time, we suffer and not them. They should suffer. With respect, 1 say Your Honour should crack down on them.
Some of us, perhaps, have an excuse for being a little long winded and stuttering a little, since we are new in the House, but members sitting on the front bench over there have no excuse and Your Honour has done nothing about it. 1 think you should, because we are suffering from the effect of these long answers.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. NYSTROM-LENGTHY PREAMBLES TO QUESTIONS PUT DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) said he hesitated even to raise this matter as a point of order. There are two considerations in play here all the time. One of them is an attempt to proportion participation in the question period, which has really been quite an exciting part of my responsibility in this Parliament, much more so than in the last. But trying to apportion it with mathematical precision does not always work. There will be some days when, if we tried to measure the participation of members by a mathematical formula, we would find that one party was slightly ahead of another. I have always been quite careful that if participation from the back benches of any party is prejudiced as a result of long-winded questions or answers from the front bench, that that prejudice stay in the same party as it originated in. The fact that I was not able to do this with extreme precision today can be laid to the lengthy answers which needed to be given. That is very difficult to assess. Sometimes questions can be asked very quickly but the answers are long, not because they are drawn out deliberately
Order Paper Questions
but because sometimes they have to be long. That is very difficult to judge.
I do not think we can try to argue on the floor exactly how this should be done with mathematical precision every day, but I certainly understand and appreciate the sentiments of hon. members who have expressed themselves so far. I see the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) is seeking the floor. This is one matter, I am sure, they cannot blame on the Creditistes because they were not up today and they were not up yesterday. I am sure he wanted to make that point clear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
Is it the intention of the House to consider more than one motion at the same time, or does the House prefer to take them one at a time? The one motion then, the motion of Mr. Stevens which I have just read.
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words about the supplementary estimates and make some comments in particular with respect to the whole area of labour, the whole field of employment opportunities in Canada. I want to take the opportunity, using this motion, to place some thoughts on the record because I think they are extremely apropos at this point in time.
Since 1979, the proportion of the national work force employed in the manufacturing sector has fallen from 26 per cent to 19 per cent. In 1970, 21 per cent of our exports consisted of manufactured goods, whereas today the figure has fallen to 10 per cent. In 1970, our trade deficit in manufactured goods was $3 billion and now the figure has increased to more than $11 billion. Foreign ownership of the Canadian economy continues. It dominates our economy. Petroleum, base metals, rubber, cars, electrical products, resources in general, are all foreign-controlled. This means the profits and dividends, the licence fees, the interest payments and the management fees must all leave the country. Indeed, that is the greatest problem with respect to our current account deficit.
I believe that when on May 22 some 37 per cent of the electorate of Canada voted for the Conservative party and that party formed a government, these people expected a change. They expected a new direction. During that campaign the Conservative party pointed out very correctly that inflation was indeed a very serious problem for working Canadians.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: It was public enemy No. 1.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
Yes, that is right. They also pointed out that unemployment was the twin brother, or the twin sister, depending on your orientation, of inflation and that these are extremely serious problems. The fact of the matter is that the government which now sits opposite is acting on the same philosophy and pursuing exactly the same policies as the government it replaced, a government which followed them for 16 years and, before that, for 106-odd years, or whatever. It is a dangerous policy. It is one which says government has no place in the board rooms of the nation and, in effect, that the government ought not to interfere in the private sector, that the government ought not to involve itself in economic management. This has created the situation we face today.
I do not think it gives us much comfort when we look at the front benches opposite and see the who's who of the corporate world sitting on those benches. These are the very people who have created the problems in this country. The corporate interests in Canada today are not interested in Canada or the Canadian people. They are not interested in the welfare of

November 8, 1979
Supply
Canadians. They are interested in their own narrow concerns of accruing greater profits and diversification of the industries to which they owe their loyalty. There is no doubt they are prepared to sell their mothers-in-law if the price is right. It seems to me they would sell anything, if anything was for sale in this country.
One has only to look at the latest report of FIRA to see how quickly they would abandon this country, take their profits and run. When we look at the front benches of this government we see the incestuous relationship between government and the corporate world. We have a finance minister who is the scion of an entrepreneurial family in Newfoundland. He used to be a Liberal. He started his own party. He crossed the floor, back and forth three times in the Newfoundland legislature. Today he sits here saying he is a neo-Tory. Sounds to me more like he is a suppository.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: We go down the line and we see the "happy hacker", the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) and the little hackers around him. He is the man who failed as a potential president of the Bank of Western Canada.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: That is why he wants to sell off profitable Crown corporations.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
He is a failed banker, and he talks in this House about selling off-privateering-businesses which Canada was forced to go into in order to preserve Canadian jobs because foreign-owned companies were closing down and laying off Canadian workers.
Then there is the economic adviser to the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark), the eminence grise, Jim Gillies, formerly member of Parliament for Don Valley. When he was a member of Parliament he said in a speech in Toronto that there was nothing wrong with our being hewers of wood and drawers of water. That role is being played out on the Tory benches today.
The hon. member for Scarborough West is the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Wightman). I received a little notice the other day from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. The association was congratulating the parliamentary secretary on his appointment. The notice said, "As you all know, Bill was our industrial relations director for many years". It must have been a manifestation of the sense of humour of the Prime Minister which made him appoint the hon. member for Scarborough West to the position of Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour. Is it not wonderful for labour to know that its future and its interests lie in the hands of a former water boy for the Canadian Manufacturers' Association?
Then there is the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ritchie). He is a former big wheel at Imperial Oil. He sits in the back smiling. He should smile. The profits of oil companies today would put a smile on the face of any

parliamentary secretary, especially if he came from Bay Street.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) was a member of a law firm which acted for Inco. We all know what Inco did to the Sudbury basin and about its commitment to job creation in this country. The minister has hired as his policy adviser Elizabeth Parr Bond, who was a big wheel at Inco.
The Conservative party has among its caucus research staff a chap named Walter Gray, another Inco boy. They are all finding homes now. They have come out of Bay Street or the Toronto-Dominion Centre, and now they are all living here in Ottawa. Thank God that nest across the street burned down.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
But now they are living on Parliament Hill; God help us!
Someone once told me that the Rideau Club was well located beside the American embassy. In the one building policies were made, and in the other building they were fired. The people making policy for Canadians now are making policy which has a bias. Let me give examples of the kinds of things which take place. I have outlined why hon. members opposite are helpless to do anything. The system needs to be challenged. Those who control the purse strings of the nation, those who are surrogates to those on Bay Street, are in no position to challenge the economic structure. Every day they say that we have to depend on the private sector to create employment.
I have never known of a corporation which was in the business of job creation. On the contrary, the business of business is business. Somebody said that in the House the other day. Therefore, the job of a corporation is not to create employment. Its job is to maximize profits and minimize costs. That is a legitimate undertaking, but what is legitimate for government? A legitimate government undertaking would be to plan the economy so that it expands and creates employment opportunities. There has to be a strategy. There have to be some rules. You either play by the rules or you go away; you do not play on the team any more.
If an immigrant came to this country and did not act in its best interests, he would be deported. That is fair ball. Those are the rules. But we have multinationals which come into this country and behave as if it is their private playground. Whenever a government says anything, they threaten, bribe and cajole. If they are not happy, they put their capital on strike. We saw that when the oil companies wanted an increase about three years ago. They took up their drills and this and that and took them to the Arabian Sea. Then we said, "Oh, boys, don't go away, we will give you a few more billions". Like the swallows returning to Capistrano, lo and behold, they came back because the price was right. The Canadian people paid it, and they still are.
Indeed, as a result of three proposals with regard to the Income Tax Act they can be paid more money to drill dry
November 8, 1979

holes than actually to discover oil. That is the way it is. They have come into Canada and done exactly what they wanted. Let me give a specific example. Everyone knows the famous IT and T. We have seen that company perform in Chile and throughout Latin America. It came to the north shore of the St. Lawrence at Port Cartier. It was going to build a pulp and paper mill. It was supposed to be a modern operation. The federal government forked over S23 million. The provincial government forked over $100 million. Every time there is a problem, we throw money at it. So, IT and T came. The plant is now six years old. What did the company do? It just shut the plant down. The plant was appropriate for Georgia and Virginia, but it was not very appropriate for the north shore of the St. Lawrence. A whole set of problems was created. The solution was to close the plant down, and 1,300 workers are out of work.
The Minister of Finance is sitting over there with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. McGrath). I would have to call them the odd couple. Both of them are from Newfoundland. I recall the situation at St. Lawrence, Newfoundland where an Alcan fluorspar mine closed down and put 400 workers out of work. That represented the whole working community because that was the only operation in St. Lawrence. They are out of work. They are on unemployment insurance. In the case of the IT and T plant in Port Cartier, 1,300 workers went on to the rolls. There have been other examples of operations being closed down. Multinationals do not like to be pressured. They want to get all the benefits and advantages, so they cajole and threaten and elect their own to the House of Commons so that they can continue. It seems that there is no will to challenge that structure. There is no will to challenge the suggestion that Canada must jump every time multinationals decide they need more for their coffers. That is not acceptable.
Let us consider another example, the shipbuilding industry in this country. I point out that 40 per cent of the workers in the Canadian shipbuilding industry are located in the province of Quebec. The Prime Minister has said in this House that he does not want to get into the referendum debate in Quebec because he thinks actions speak louder than words. I agree with him. In effect, we could say as well that inaction speaks louder than words. Here we have a situation where 1,700 jobs have disappeared in the Quebec shipyards in the last year and another 3,500 jobs are threatened.
I want to say that that kind of situation undermines the interests of Canada. It is more destructive than any rabble-rousing speech by any separatist in the province of Quebec or the province of Alberta. I think that that is a very destructive situation because, in the long run, a person has to decide if there is more benefit to be derived from being part of a united Canada, with all the strength and diversity that that carries, or if it is better to go it alone. They cannot do any worse. It seems to me that the Prime Minister has an opportunity here in
Supply
assisting the shipbuilding industry in the province of Quebec or, for that matter, in eastern Canada.
There is a lot of talk about having our own merchant marine, and there are some navy ships to be built, but action must be taken now. These cannot just be promises which are going to be held up and recycled election after election. There has to be some action taken to get this going. We certainly saw the demise of the merchant navy under the Liberal party when it formed the government. Now we have Tweedledee out and Tweedledum in, and they are telling us that they will bring back the merchant navy.
So, true to form, they set up a committee to study the matter. They must be the most studious group over there, because everything is being studied. When they were in opposition, they had all the answers. They did not need any studies. In fact, they accused the Liberals of always doing studies on everything. Now they are in government, it turns out they do not have the answers at all. They have embarked on make work projects for all the backbench Tories who did not get cabinet posts. They give out a press blurb that Joe so-and-so from the back benches has been appointed chairman of a committee to study ingrown toenails and, lo and behold, he gets the committee going.
Now they are saying we should have a merchant marine and that is how we are going to stimulate the shipbuilding industry in Canada. As a result of that campaign promise, the leader of our party wrote to the Prime Minister and received the following reply on October 16, 1979:
Dear Mr. Broadbent:
I have your letter of October 1, 1979, regarding the Halifax shipyard and Panamax drydock.
You will be pleased to know this government places a high priority on the improvement of the Canadian shipbuilding and repair industry. The economic development committee of cabinet, under the chairmanship of the Minister of State for Economic Development, is presently reviewing the shipbuilding and repair industry in general, and the Panamax drydock in particular.
Given the urgency of this matter, I expect the committee will bring forward their recommendations at a very early date.
I take this opportunity to express my thanks for your support in our continuing efforts to establish an economically viable merchant marine.
Yours sincerely,
Joe Clark.
"We have set up a study and we are going to study the merchant marine now", they say. When they were in the opposition, they said: "we must have a merchant marine now". I ask, what is the study for? It seems to me that what we have to do now is to look at ways and means. We should lay out a plan. We all saw the leader of the Conservative party meeting with all his minions at some resort around here with lots of books, and those were the blueprints for change. Now we are finding out that all these problems have to be studied as if they had to look at the reason why we need a merchant marine after all. While they are doing that, jobs are going down the tube in this country, jobs are disappearing. In effect, this government sits on its hands and says, "We are studying the problem".

November 8, 1979
Supply
We asked a question today with regard to an order for the construction of a ferry which the CN is placing, a ferry to be used in eastern Canada. Where are they looking to construct [DOT] the ferry? They are looking to place the order for its construction in the United States. For example, this country needs legislation which would say that if we are going to build a merchant marine and if we are going to spend any money on shipbuilding, the building and the spending should be done in Canada. We should delineate that policy very clearly. After all, Bill Davis, when he discovered that the street cars he was buying would be cheaper in Montreal than Thunder Bay, forced TCC to purchase them from Thunder Bay because there was a need to create jobs in northwestern Ontario in particular. So, in effect, the Ontario government intervened by directing job creation.
It seems to me that we need to have a policy. It is surprising to note-it is not surprising for me and for those of us who live in the Sudbury basin, but it is surprising for people who are not from there-that 50 per cent of the nickel mined in the Sudbury basin leaves the Sudbury basin in a semi-processed state, in matt form. Then it goes to the United States and it goes to Wales and is finished in its final form, following which it is sold back to us. It seems to me that at this point in time we need to have a clearly defined policy to direct that our resources will be refined to their final stage at the place where they are mined. This should also apply to our forestry resource. We are still shipping our pulp in a semi-processed state from the east coast of Canada to Europe, and we buy back fine paper. It seems to me, for example, that our economic strategy should clearly define that Canadian resources must be refined by Canadians in Canada.
It is becoming very clear that the employment factor is in the manufacturing sector, not in the ripping out of resources. The ripping out of resources is capital intensive, but jobs are in the refining and manufacturing of the resource.
The government has done an analysis of research and development. That is another area where we do not have a clearly defined policy. They should no longer be studying what has caused problems in the economy. When they were in the opposition, they knew what the problems were. What we should be doing now is putting in place some policies to achieve full employment.
We have the spectacle of the President of the Treasury Board saying the government are going to sell de Havilland and Canadair, keeping in mind that de Havilland and Cana-dair came as a direct result of the analysis which I have just given in terms of foreign ownership. Those were two industries whose foreign owners decided they were no longer going to keep them in Canada and so they decided to close them down.
It was the fear of all those jobs being lost which caused the Canadian government to step in and take those two companies over and build up these industries, which gave us some expertise in the aeronautical industry. Now that the gang of 138 is in-

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
The gang of 136 is now saying, "We have to privateer these companies." The suffix "ize" should only be added to one noun, and that is "fertile".
It seems that when they are talking like this, saying they are going to privatize or privateer de Havilland, one should remember that the President of the Treasury Board, in a meeting with the United Auto Workers which represents the workers of de Havilland and who are concerned about jobs and Canadians working, and not interested in Canadians going on unemployment insurance and on welfare, said he is not prepared to give them guarantees. Representatives of that union attempted to get some guarantees from the minister that if the government proceeded with the sale it would be sold to Canadian owners and that whoever buys the industry will not be allowed to pick up the plant and put it in some other part of the country, creating a great deal of hardship for the thousands of employees of those operations. The President of the Treasury Board in his usual mild and self-effacing way told them he was not prepared to give those guarantees.
When the minister was pressed to bring the matter to Parliament he got into a great big spiel about how they actually came into public ownership. He mentioned some dollar item in the estimates as though that was relevant. What is relevant is the situation now, not what was done previously. In effect, this government has embarked on the principle that Parliament is supreme and that Parliament is the place where these decisions should be made. Indeed, we had the example of a bill passed in one day just two weeks ago making legal an increase in postal rates which has been in effect now for a year. The argument was that it was done by order in council under the Financial Administration Act, but Parliament should decide the increase in postal rates.
These corporations come under the Financial Administration Act and they are infinitely more important than an increase in the postal rate from 14 to 17 cents, yet we observe the arrogance of the President of the Treasury Board in ignoring Parliament and denying Parliament the opportunity to debate the matter. He now sits there and smiles. This is not a smiling matter, it is an extremely important matter, particularly to the 23,000 workers of de Havilland.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: How many?

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: There are 23,000 in all their various operations. They are concerned about what happens if that plant and those operations are sold and relocated somewhere else in the country. That is extremely important to them. The President of the Treasury Board can laugh all he wants. He does not have to worry about where his next pay cheque is coming from because he knows darn well that he can move on to the Senate. He knows that if he was defeated he would go to the Senate. He knows they will find a niche for him somewhere in the corporate structure.

speechtext:
He will become a bank president.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
We are coming to the Bank Act in a minute. It seems to me that this is a perfect example of what this government is attempting to do. They are putting us back into the hands of the very people who created the problems. You know what happens when these corporations close down and move on. People go on unemployment insurance when that happens and this government is now tightening up on unemployment insurance.
These fellows to our right did their trick when the Conservatives were in opposition. The Conservatives in opposition opposed the previous Bill C-14, having to do with the latest changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) carried out a campaign in eastern Canada pointing out how terrible the Liberals were to bring in changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, changes that would have devastating effects on the poor people of eastern Canada. Now that they have been elected and are sitting in the government benches, one would have thought they would at least have scotched that. But no, what they have done is continue the changes and allow them to come into effect. Those changes are detrimental.
This government has no control over the economy and is allowing these corporations to put Canadians out of work. When that happens Canadians go on the dole, on unemployment insurance. When that happens the government turns around and blames the victims for the conditions in which they find themselves. They start tearing away at the humanity of fellow Canadians, men and women. They start saying things like they are ripping off the unemployment insurance system, they are stealing, they are lazy, they are young people and do not want to work, they are only women, secondary earners, and so on. This is a very dehumanizing thing to Canadians who are unemployed. All this makes these people feel guilty about receiving unemployment insurance. They became unemployed because of unilateral decisions on the part of corporations.
I know the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander) is a very nice, hearty, hail and bluff fellow. He gets up and says, through an intermediary, an unknown official in the labour department, that he is concerned that he does not have enough importance in the cabinet. I think he is in the outer ring. Some members are inners and some are outers, and apparently he is an outer. He wants to get to be an inner.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: It's an in and out house.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
An "in house" and "out house", I get it. That minister wants to enhance his role and that of his department. He says it only has a budget of $40 million and "X" number of man-years of employees, so he wants to take over more of the responsibilities of the Minister of Employment and Immigration. He makes a good argument. He says: "After all, we are both paid the same ministerial salary, allowance and everything else so why should I not share the work?" He does not have to take anything away from the Ministry of Employment and Immigration. He should bring in
Supply
some legislation that puts some flesh on the labour structure of this country.
For example, there ought to be adequate notice of shutdown. There should not be this business of a company deciding that six weeks from today it is going to close down its plant. In some countries corporations are not allowed to do that. In some countries the notice for a shutdown or layoff in some cases is a year or more, so that if there is something structurally wrong they can look for alternate ways to employ the workers, or to change the operation and retain the workers.
The Minister of Labour has a wonderful opportunity. We have the Bank Act. The banks want some changes. They want security for Canadian banks. They do not like foreign banks. They want security for themselves in respect of operating in this country. However, they will not provide any security for their employees vis-a-vis the efforts to organize bank employees. The banks have fought tooth and nail against the organization of bank workers into unions.
What has the Minister of Labour been doing? He does not have changes to the labour code he intends to bring in to provide the Rand formula which has been accepted in this country for so many years. As a result, we have situations in which the banks refuse to negotiate in good faith. They will not agree to the Rand formula with regard to the collective agreement.
There are many changes that must be made to the labour code to enhance the working place, to make the workplace a more human place. For example, there is much to be done in the field of occupational health and safety. There are thousands of chemicals that come into the workplace in this country every month, yet there is no pre-testing. The only testing is in the acutal use of those materials and the subsequent results years later when we fight a rearguard action to improve the quality of the workplace. There is a whole new spectre with regard to stress in the workplace, a new danger in the workplace, but that whole area has not been looked at by the Minister of Labour.
For example, part IV of the labour code says that the minister may set up health and safety committees in the workplace. There is nothing in the labour code which says that it is mandatory. To date the minister has not set up one health and safety committee in a workplace under federal jurisdiction. It seems that he has so many problems to deal with, such as the question of technological change and the impact of technological change on the work style of workers in this country. There are so many things that should be done, but the Minister of Labour has not touched any of them.
It seems to me, as we take a look at what has been happening in Canada, that there is no reason to have any confidence in this government. It seems that they are carrying on the disastrous policies established by their predecessors. This government is not prepared to challenge the corporate structure in Canada, to place Canada first, to take a firm stand with respect to economic planning or to step in and say

November 8, 1979
Supply
that the government has a role to play in the planning of the economy. All these things must happen, otherwise we will continue to rip out our resources, and to lose, therefore, many job opportunities.
Interest rates are rising, Mr. Speaker. The government says that we are locked into the American interest rate structure, and that if their interest rate rises, so must ours. What has happened is that it has sneaked continentalism in through the back door. The effect of high interest rates on industry is illustrated in British Columbia where the Weldwood plant has had to lay off 700 workers because interest rates have made it uneconomical for the plant to keep these people.
This government has said that things will get worse before they get better. It is the old story, the operation was successful but the patient died. The government keeps saying that raising the interest rates is the way to fight inflation, but in fact it causes inflation. How does one bring inflation down by allowing interest rates to rise? When they were in opposition, it was wonderful to hear the Conservatives make all their arguments against rising interest rates, but now that they are the government, they say that we are locked in.
If one looks at the answers in Hansard given by the minister of finance of the previous government with regard to interest rates, one will find that they are exactly the same answers the current Minister of Finance has been giving out. The government does not have a new approach or a new deal. All they say is that we must renew initiatives and let Canadians pull themselves up by their bootstraps. It is operation bootstraps. It is forward into the past. That is the myth today, that somehow or other having a free enterprise system and competition will solve our economic problems. It will not solve our problems.
This government has brought in the supplementary estimates which were introduced by the previous government, but they could easily be the supplementary estimates of this government because they have accepted holus-bolus the basic philosophy on which Canada is run, economically speaking.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recognizing that the NDP has decided that they would speak on this motion, I want to put on record the reason my party will not participate in the debate. It is because we would prefer to wait and have our day in Committee of the Whole. We are prepared today to go into Committee of the Whole on the bill with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. McGrath). It is not because we are not interested or that we agree that the House should give passage to this matter of supply without asking any questions of the government about what they have done. Or I should say what they have not done, because they really have not done very much. That is the position of our party.
We recognize that the NDP has decided otherwise, and we do not question that. They see it as their duty to participate in this debate. What we want to do is get at these ministers and bring them before Parliament and the eyes of the public to show the public what this government has not done in the past five months.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a couple of remarks in response to the remarks made by the poverty-stricken member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). I share his concern that when government contracts are given out, we ought to preserve as many jobs as possible for Canadians. The hon. member referred to the proposed ferry to be built by Canadian National and said that it ought to be built by Canadians if at all possible.
My mind then went back several years when the hon. member for Nickel Belt was on a Commonwealth Parliamentary Association trip to Sri Lanka. The hon. member came back with a Persian rug, much like the Persian rugs found over in the Rideau Club which he eschewed so much. When the hon. member landed in London, he went straight from the airport to the English Channel in order to catch a ferry to France so that he could buy a headlamp for his French car. It was not a Renault or Peugeot but a Citroen. That is the hon. member's way of preserving Canadian jobs. I hope when he hires help to look after his race horse that it is Canadian help.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know where the hon. member got this idea. He may have been on some sort of Arabian Night's dream. I do not know on what basis he makes those accusations about my purchasing non-Canadian items. I do not frequent the South African embassy, and therefore do not have an opportunity to enjoy South African wines. I do not know what the hon. member is talking about.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the point raised by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), I would like to make it very clear that I support him completely. We would sooner get into Committee of the Whole and call certain ministers to reply in this Parliament to specific questions, rather than make long speeches and get no answers. The members of the NDP have chosen, which is their right, to Filibuster on this bill and not go into Committee of the Whole. As the official opposition we will watch their actions, and if they continue to filibuster we will also put up some speakers.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this matter, but then I heard the remarks of the Liberal whip.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: What is that in your hand?

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
I will tell you what it is in a minute. The Liberal whip has said that the member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), by making an eloquent and tremendous speech, is leading my party on a filibuster. I would like to know, as the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) asked, what the hon. member's definition is of filibuster.
We are dealing with supplementary estimates here which are very important. I think the reason the Liberals do not wish to participate is that they are embarrassed. We are dealing with estimates proposed by the previous Liberal government. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) is nodding

November 8, 1979

his head. He is now piloting some Liberal goodies through the House of Commons. Perhaps that is why they are embarrassed to speak. They are looking for any excuse to avoid participating in this debate.
I want to say to my Liberal friends that some very important things are happening in this country, and so it does no harm to spend a few hours on this stage of the debate. When government members were in opposition they used to do this quite often.
1 should like to refer to one issue which I think is very important, Mr. Speaker, and that is the speech made in Calgary yesterday, by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazan-kowski), who is responsible to the Canadian Wheat Board, to the United Grain Growers. We are dealing today with the estimates that concern transportation, the movement of grain and things that are very important to farmers in the west. 1 should like to quote one or two things from that speech. The minister said:
I am frustrated-
I suppose he is frustrated at being a member of that cabinet. He continued:
-at present because we are passing up sales-perhaps worth $1 billion per year-because of limitations in our transportation system. I can't help thinking what it would mean to producers and to Canada if we were exporting 50 per cent more grain and oilseeds. There would be a tremendous increase in cash flow and net income for producers. The additional sales would earn Canada $2-$3 billion a year in badly needed foreign exchange. . . . And it would generate an additional $4 billion a year in domestic economic activity.
I want to make the point here that we are dealing with a resolution on the estimates of the old Liberal government. The administration which Otto Lang headed as minister of transport cost this country literally billions and billions of dollars per year for the movement of grain. The Minister of Transport says that about $1 billion was lost last year because the grain could not be moved, and an extra $4 billion was lost as a result of reduced economic activity that would have been attendant upon the movement of the grain.
1 think it is important to register our dissatisfaction with the amount of money provided in the supplementary estimates for the movement of grain. I want to make it clear that I expect the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie)-the Ayatollah Cros-bie-to include several hundreds of millions of dollars to repair the branch lines on the prairies and to purchase hopper cars when he brings down his budget. The Minister of Transport is complaining that the grain was not moved due to the inefficient system left the country by 16 years of Liberal party rule.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
1 hope the Minister of Finance realizes that his backbenchers are applauding, meaning they agree this should be done. I see him nodding-I can hear him from here! I hope he takes very seriously representations made by the backbenchers of his party and by members of this party. We cannot afford to lose $4 billion per year. It would seem to me
Supply
good economic sense to invest a few hundred million dollars in order to reap an additional $4 billion per year in economic activity in the west.
I have another concern about the speech made by the Minister of Transport in Calgary yesterday, Mr. Speaker. He spoke of the possibility of getting rid of the Crow rate or changing it. He said that if there is any change of application of the Crow rate it will have to be coupled with adequate service guarantees. This morning, speaking on the CBC, he elaborated on the possibility that the Conservative party may change the Crow rate. I do not know what kind of change they are thinking of, so I think it is important that someone in the Conservative party should make their stand clear as soon as possible.
I should like to take a moment to point out to members of the House how important the Crow rate is to Canadian farmers, Mr. Speaker. Many years ago the CPR was given a lot of land, mineral rights and property. In return for that, they guaranteed to haul the farmers' grain at a set price in the years ahead. That price is set in the statutes of this country, and to the farmers that is very important. If the Crow rate was varied it would cost farmers from 400 per cent to 600 per cent more to haul grain to market, compared to the cost for the equivalent distance in the United States.
During the election campaign last May the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) said that if the Conservative party was elected it would guarantee retention of the Crow rate. The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) has not given that assurance, however, and now the Minister of Transport is saying that they are considering getting rid of or changing the rate.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the spirit of Otto Lang lives; the spirit of Otto Lang is reincarnated in the Minister of Transport!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: Be serious.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
I am being very serious, Mr. Speaker. Many members of the Conservative party have spoken about abolishing the Crow rate. The Hall commission report, however, recommended the retention and extension of the Crow rate to cover processed raw materials.
Just a week or so ago I heard the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) comment on the radio that the Crow rate should be changed. The Conservative governments in Alberta and Manitoba have spoken about altering the Crow rate. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hargrave) has said that the Crow rate should be altered. As well, the newly appointed western grain transportation coordinator, Hugh Horner, brother of the famous Jack, has spoken of the possibility of abolishing the Crow rate.
Where does this government stand, Mr. Speaker? Do they stand behind the Crow rate? Do they stand behind the farmers of western Canada? The member for Lisgar says, "Oh, baloney". I am sure he knows whereof he speaks because he speaks a lot of baloney about Crow rates. I am sure that the

November 8, 1979
Supply
Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources would be one of the first to tell him that.
There are a number of other issues that are important when it comes to moving grain, Mr. Speaker. A few weeks ago the hon. member for Lisgar made a statement to the effect that the port of Churchill should be abandoned; that we should not haul grain to the port of Churchill. I wonder if that is Conservative party policy? During the election campaign the Conservative party advocated using the port of Churchill, and indeed that its use be increased. Where do they stand on the question now?
These are questions that should be answered when we are dealing with the supplementary estimates. Perhaps the great Minister of Finance or the President of the Treasury Board could enlighten us before the debate ends.
I should like to point out to the House, Mr. Speaker, what the effect would be if the Crow rate were abolished. According to the 1977 Snavely report, if the Crow rate were abolished prairie farmers would lose $290 million, and with spin-off effects this would take over $1 billion out of the western economy. We can take the town of Wakaw, in the Prince Albert area, as an example of what this would mean. The Crow rate from Wakaw to Vancouver is 24 cents per 100 pounds of grain. The CN charge for grain on domestic shipments to Vancouver is $3.12 per hundred pounds-or 13 times Crow.
It is important for the government to tell us where they stand on Crow rates, Mr. Speaker, because on November 19 the people of Wakaw will be voting in a byelection. One of the questions they are asking now is where the Conservative party stands on Crow and whether they will have to pay 13 times more than they do now to ship their grain if they keep this government in power. Where do they stand? I ask that question because we have had conflicting stories from ministers across the way. The Minister of Transport wants them reviewed. The minister of energy said that the Crow would be guaranteed. I want the Minister of Finance or someone responsible on the other side to tell us precisely where the Conservative party stands.
There are many more things one can say about the supplementary estimates that are before us. There are many more things that are important to prairie farmers. But on the Crow itself, which is perhaps the most important and emotional issue out there, the Minister of Transport is talking about the possibility of the Crow benefit being extended to farmers in other ways. For example, he said that perhaps the money set aside to maintain branch lines could be used to subsidize the farmers. If he used that money, what happens to the branch line?
These are questions that have to be answered. Is it the intention of the government across the way to abandon these branch lines? In the election campaign we were told that any line would be kept open if the elevator company on that line was willing to provide service and have a decent elevator to

handle the farmers' grain. Now we have a one-man task force appointed by the Conservative party, namely, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), who is studying rail line abandonment and what to do about that question.
These are important questions because the previous Liberal government has intentionally allowed the grain handling system in this country to become run down over the last 16 years. Yesterday in Calgary the Minister of Transport said that the Crow rate may be abolished, or that the Crow rate in this country may be changed.
Next we come to the Wheat Board. We are dealing here with supplementary estimates, and in that connection I include the Canadian Wheat Board. I want to know what the government's intentions are regarding the Canadian Wheat Board. There are some members who are very powerful in the Conservative party. The hon. member for Lisgar is listened to as the eyes and ears of the Minister of Transport. It has been said that we should have more competition, more free enterprise and more of the open market, and that the port of Churchill should not be utilized. Does that mean we will have less and less for the farmers in the estimates when it comes to the Wheat Board or when it comes to using the port of Churchill?

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: Wait and see.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
The hon. member across the way says wait and see. I am very nervous about what I am going to see. That is why 1 am not waiting before registering my objections to the direction which the Conservative party and the Government of Canada seem to be taking.
The minister who yields a lot of power, the minister in charge of privateering, is privateering almost everything. I want to know what plans there are for the Wheat Board, for the Crow rate and for the Farm Credit Corporation. These are things that are most important to prairie farmers and for which they fought for years and years.
I am sure you will know, being a farmer yourself, that the Hall commission recommended the Wheat Board be given more power to co-ordinate grain transportation and that the grain movement co-ordinator should be a Wheat Board employee. What did the Conservative party do? The government appointed Hugh Horner. As I said, little Jack's brother was appointed to that powerful position of grain transportation co-ordinator.
What about Hugh Horner? I have no doubt the guy is sincere, intelligent and competent. But what is his attitude vis-a-vis the Canadian Wheat Board? I think he is biased against the Canadian Wheat Board. Hugh Horner was quoted by the press as saying that he would like to see the quota system abolished. That is the very system that creates equality of delivery opportunity for farmers, be they small or large. Hugh Horner would like to abolish that system. It seems to me that he now has immense power in his hands.
Where does the Minister of Transport stand when it comes to some important issues like the quota system, the Wheat Board, quarterly marketing, the Crow rate, the Hall commis-
November 8, 1979

sion report, the Snavely report, the port of Churchill, etc? These things are vital and important to the farmers on the prairies. 1 ask again, where does he stand? All we have to do to get an answer is look at the supplementary estimates. We know where Otto Lang and the Liberal party stood. The Minister of Transport in a speech made in Calgary said that we probably lost $1 billion worth of sales last year. When I was in China recently the Chinese pointed out that we could transplant hearts, fly to the moon and do all of those marvellous things, yet we could not haul grain on time from the farmer's granary to the ship. The Chinese asked why we could not do that.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: Did you speak in Chinese?

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
I know my Chinese is not as good as that of the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), but the Chinese were concerned. The Chinese have now turned to the United States for grain and will sign the first grain contract with them in years. I am very happy the Americans are establishing normal relations with the Chinese, but 1 am also very concerned that Canada and its farmers will lose potential markets because we do not have a grain handling system.
How can we solve this problem? That is what 1 am asking the Conservative party across the way. 1 ask where does it stand on these important issues. 1 want a definitive statement from the Prime Minister of this country about where he stands on Crow. If the Crow rate goes, so go the small farmers. Some Conservatives have said, "Well, you can pay the Crow benefit." In other words, one takes the cost difference between the commercial cost of shipping grain from point A. 1 use the example of Wakaw where the cost is 13 times higher than the Crow rate. One can take the difference between that and the statutory rate and reimburse the farmer. Over 100,000 farmers will be reimbursed in the form of a cheque sent in the mail. I think that is a very complicated, bureaucratic and indeed potentially dangerous way of making sure the farmer gets the Crow rate benefit. It is very bureaucratic.
With members such as the President of the Treasury Board who is interested in cutting back on government spending and hacking away at government expenses, who will guarantee that that minister or one of his successors will not decide some day to cut back on the Crow benefit program? There is no guarantee that that will not happen.
The railways are interested in a profit and will charge a higher commercial rate for branch lines than they will for main lines. They will charge a higher rate for a little town such as Wakaw than they will for a city such as Prince Albert. Then we will have defacto abandonment of the rail lines and defacto abandonment of the branch lines. These issues are important. They are vital to western Canada.
By spending a few minutes this afternoon on the Liberal supplementary estimates before the House and introduced by the party across the way, I have pointed out some of the problems we have had in the past that have not been solved. However, I see in a speech made by the Minister of Transport
Supply
that the Conservative party may have some solutions, but the solutions may be more of a problem than the existing situation for many farmers on the prairies.
In conclusion, if the Conservative party goes ahead to abandon or change the Crow rate, it will be in for a fight. It will be in for a fight not only from the people on the prairies and the NDP and its federal caucus, but also from the wheat pools, the co-operatives and the progressive farm groups. It will be in for a fight like it has never had from the government of Saskatchewan.
I serve that as notice to the party which sits across the way. They must not tamper with the Crow rate. They must keep the Canadian Wheat Board strong. They must strengthen the board as a co-operative agency so that it will handle the grain of the farmers on an equal basis. They must retain a quota system so that all farmers, rich or poor, close to delivery points or far, with an early harvest or a late harvest, have an equal opportunity to deliver their grain. We must not follow the law of the jungle, first come first served, or the law of capital, the elephant and the mouse, where the big guy outmuscles the small.
These issues are important. I hope that before this debate is over someone in the Conservative party will stand up to tell us where they stand on these issues which are crucial to the people of my province and region of Canada.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my belief that the supplementary estimates have failed to meet the needs of my constituents and of the people in the rest of the country. Perhaps I can briefly describe my constituency in order to help members better understand my remarks on these estimates.
The Churchill constituency encompasses the northern two-thirds of the province of Manitoba. It has over seven degrees of latitude, over 400 miles, and 12 degrees of longitude. There are many Indian reserves and a number of Metis communities. The Churchill constituency has five mining towns, including Flin Flon and Thompson. The Pas, also in the constituency of Churchill, is a historic community for fur trading and now has some agriculture, the CN and forest products which provide employment for that region.
In The Pas, the Manfor project, formerly called CFI, is an example of what happens when government relies on and gives millions to private enterprise in order to provide employment and develop our resources. An official inquiry and the courts have proven that we were robbed blind. The case was so bad that the present premier of Manitoba forgot that he went to Zurich to sign the original agreement-a very poor memory.
Also within my constituency is the port of Churchill. It is an orphan of Tory and Liberal governments. It has been deserted by its parents. Why has the port not been developed? Why is grain not in the port at the beginning of the shipping season? Why has the CN line to Churchill not been fixed?
Why does the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) call the port a luxury we cannot afford? He was appointed by his

November 8, 1979
Supply
government to look into grain handling. Why does he speak to the press about an issue of this nature, presumably speaking for his party and the government? The minister had to correct and deny the allegations and comments of the hon. member for Lisgar.
The port of Churchill is important not only to my constituency but to the prairie provinces and, indeed, the country. We cannot allow that port to be downgraded by this or any other government. Northern farmers as well as those in the south of Saskatchewan use that port because of its benefit to the people and farmers in those regions.
When the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) talked about being from the riding of the dinosaurs, and that it is also the home of the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark), 1 presume he meant to connect those two matters.
Churchill is the fossil of political promises made by members opposite and by members of the Liberal party. The people there were promised heaven but were given hell. These supplementary estimates are just a stopping place, purgatory. They and the main estimates provide to the people of the community of Churchill and the larger constituency of Churchill only a brief respite from the economic domination and damnation provided by these governments. Our resources are developed, our land is scarred and flooded, but the real values of these economic activities are not of benefit to the residents of the north, be they white or native, especially native. The native population is not being employed in the mines, at least in any great number, or at the permanent hydroelectric stations, and the great CFI giveaway limited the access of native groups in terms of harvesting our forests. They are not allowed to harvest certain areas of the north because of the agreement the Conservative government of Manitoba signed with the multinational corporations.
Within the supplementary estimates of fisheries and oceans there is no provision to develop the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. Presently Canadians buy only a very small fraction of the fish caught in northern Manitoba and in the other freshwater areas of the country. This lack of initiative of government and reliance on corporations like Safeway to provide our daily bread has meant that it is virtually impossible to buy fresh fish in my home town of Thompson, yet we are surrounded by a number of communities in which fishermen are trying to make a living. In Thompson we can buy frozen fish that has been imported from other countries but we cannot buy fresh fish. This problem was created by the present government and the previous government.
Instead of providing funds for the FFMC to expand its operations, the government in Ottawa is allowing the Manitoba government to let American buyers back into the market. If this is allowed, the fishermen in the north will again be put into economic serfdom. The FFMC want to keep out the American buyers in order that the fishermen in these communities can have a guaranteed income and be provided with an honest living. If it is allowed to go back to its previous state, the fishermen in my constituency will suffer.

While I am discussing the state of our native people, I would like to turn to the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. How can they expect to promote Indian economic development when freezing the Indian economic development fund and centralizing control of these operations? For example, in British Columbia the final control of the Indian economic development fund has been taken away from the regional director and placed in the hands of the ADM in Ottawa. Treasury Board is winning the battle of control. Soon no regional government employee will be able to do anything other than shuffle paper, pick up requests from the natives, say nothing, pass it on to Ottawa, receive it back from the bureaucrats in Ottawa, again say nothing and return it to the native people. This government claims to believe in decentralizing. However, for them decentralizing does not mean providing service on a regional basis but providing a shield to protect those who make the decisions from the people who make the requests. That is not decentralization.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
