subsubtopic: REPORT ON FEASIBILITY OF ESTABLISHING CROWN CORPORATION FOR FORESTRY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me an opportunity to say a few additional words in response to the motion of the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for the production of papers concerning the intention to establish a Crown corporation or, in his words, some other body that would in the interests of ail Canadians establish some kind of an effort toward the research and development of technology and techniques which could be brought in to manage our national forests.
In his opening remarks the hon. member spoke of the previous government's efforts to establish a national forests policy. I have followed these efforts with keen interest over quite a number of years now, and 1 cannot share the enthusiasm the hon. member brought to the House since I have never been much impressed with the efforts which were made. Indeed, since 1963, over the last decade, the efforts of the Canadian forest service have been cut in half. There is roughly about half the manpower in the Canadian forest service today as there was ten years ago. Of course, many of the scientists who carried out the research and development upon which the industry relied so heavily have left the department and what we find here today are administrators and bureaucrats. There is really no major effort at all being carried on in the area of research and development in this important industry.
The results of this kind of deterioration are very noticeable. Our world position, shown by the percentage of world markets which we once enjoyed, has declined by over 20 per cent in the last ten years and the United States' share of the world market has increased by almost the same percentage.
There are very good reasons for this. One American company alone-the Warehouser Company in the United States- spends more money annually in research and development than does the entire Canadian forest service. This has to be a matter of concern to us, particularly when one considers the crucial importance of the forest industry in our economy and its effect on the well-being of the country in general.
The forests generate more income than gas and oil, agriculture, fisheries and mining combined. Forest companies shipped last year $13 billion worth of goods; $8 billion went to export earnings and contributed to our balance of trade. Every man, woman and child in this country shares or owns the equivalent of about 20 acres of productive forest land. We have about 800 million acres of productive forest lands in Canada. Unfortunately, over that ten year period of which I spoke earlier, 60 million acres of this vital resource, this productive forest land, have been left idle. There has not been a sufficient effort to regenerate these important lands and put them back into operation.
There were some efforts made by the former government; the latest took place just before Parliament dissolved. The one we are well aware of, because the subject was raised in this House on many occasions, was the effort to privatize a very
Forestry Research
important portion of the federal research effort, namely that of the forest products lab here in Ottawa and on the west coast in Vancouver. It was proposed to turn these efforts over to private companies.
The question has to be asked: To what extent can we expect private industry to take over these efforts? I am talking about research and development which needs to be carried out to protect all our forests, to carry on the kind of husbandry which will preserve our forests in perpetuity for future generations. One is faced with this question when one takes into account the fact that last year the federal government took in $1 billion from the forest economy. In the same period of time, on an annual basis, all provinces combined take in about an equal amount, namely $1 billion. This accrues to governments in the form of revenue from taxes, leases, royalties and so on. It makes up a total of $2 billion. And now governments are telling the industry that it will have to carry on its own research and development efforts.
The industry is always prepared to assume these responsibilities providing that governments reciprocate. What the industry would want, in return, is some kind of security of tenure. It would need assurances that if the industry does the research, the regenerating, fertilizing and replanting, the results of such activities would accrue to their benefit in the future. In other words, they would seek longer tenures, ownership of forest lands and so on. It has been the policy of most of the provinces and the federal government not to give industry that kind of control over this vital resource. It is my opinion, therefore, that we should not expect the industry to carry on the research and development that is required to preserve this vital resource in perpetuity.
On this side of the House we are asking ourselves what the former government has done, how far it got in developing a national forest policy. Sadly, sir, we must report that there has really been no advance in the development of such a policy.
What needs to be done, then? Well, the present minister has already taken some important initiatives. There is presently a major review in the terms of reference given to departmental officials. There has to be a concentration and a centralization of the various jurisdictions responsible on behalf of the federal government in the forest policy area. No fewer than 26 different departments of the federal government are in some way responsible for forests. There is the Department of the Environment, DREE, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce-I could not begin to name them all. The idea is, as a result of this review, to bring back and re-establish a component of a Canadian forest service which will once again assume the responsibility for a co-ordinating role with the provinces to preserve this vital resource. That may well mean a structural change in the make up of the committees.
I have just come from the committee and I am half out of breath. Even as I speak here the minister is answering a question I posed to him in that committee. Unfortunately forestry is tied in with the important committee on the environment and fisheries and members of this House are having a difficult time running back and forth trying to determine on

November 8, 1979
Forestry Research
what day the chairman of that committee or the steering committee of that committee chooses to talk about forests. There is nothing about forestry in the estimates at all. There is no reference, no mention of forestry in this big blue book. I know the minister is very concerned about this, as I am. Structural changes are required, including the appointment of senior officials in the public service to assume responsibility and advise the minister in these important areas.
The industry is ready and stands prepared to assume and to share in the responsibility. We made recommendations to the former government on how this sharing should take place. If one fifth of the money which is paid to provincial governments in the form of royalties, or 50 cents on every thousand board feet of lumber harvested and manufactured, were returned into an effort which could be carried out by provincial and federal governments, it would mean that the 60 million acres which are presently lying idle could be regenerated over a five-year period. I am talking about a massive infusion of funds, to the tune of $250 million, which would accrue to the two governments in one year. If that amount of money which comes from private industry were matched by the provinces and by the federal government, we could indeed realize a very significant turnaround and a renewal in the commitment and responsibility we have for preserving this vital resource for future generations.
I am confident that the minister who is presently responsible is as serious as I and, I am sure, most members of the House, about bringing about this kind of structural and administrative change and about bringing about once again the pride and commitment our public servants had to this vital resource which they manage for us. I am confident that over a short period of time we will see a significant turnaround and that our industry, which once enjoyed a very unique position in the world in shipping and delivering this resource to world markets, will once again see the kind of stability and confidence they had in their endeavours before.
I am confident as well that the minister is cognizant of the crucial importance the forests have in terms of the environment and the total eco-system that generates our water and our clean air; and I am also confident that the minister is aware of the incredible importance our forests have in social areas and in tourism where forests provide the backdrop for a $250 million industry every year.
I am confident of all these things, but I am not as confident as the hon. member for Vaudreuil, who is well intentioned and who has given us this opportunity to debate this matter, that another Crown corporation or some other agency, as he suggests in his motion, could fulfil this need. People expect significant change from new governments, and I am confident that this new government is committed to recognizing our forests and our forestry efforts in light of what I have said.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON FEASIBILITY OF ESTABLISHING CROWN CORPORATION FOR FORESTRY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion in the name of the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) has very clearly proved one point: there is evidently in this House a very keen interest in and a consensus on the matter of forestry conditions in our country and perhaps even as to how those conditions could be dealt with by the federal government.
I suppose that other interventions will clarify this point further, but it seems to me that at least it can be said fairly at this point that there is a deep concern on the part of members, who in turn reflect the views of their constituents, that our forests need attention. It is surprising to some of us to be told by experts that the picture of seemingly limitless forests and woods is in good part an illusion. The national forest regeneration conference, which was held in Quebec city in October of 1977, concluded that adequate forest renewal was nothing less than an urgent economic need. The conference was attended by some 250 representatives of government, industry, the forestry profession, universities and environmental protection organizations. These representatives agreed unanimously that, as they put it in their communique, inadequate forest regeneration is:
-indeed a serious and fundamental forestry problem. This concern is not yet felt by the general public or by politicians, and there is a real need-as demonstrated by the conference-to "spread the bad news".
Studies released at the conference indicated that only about half of the statistical surplus is "economically accessible". This means that it can be harvested at a low enough cost to enable the producer to sell the end product at a viable price on the world market.
The communique went on to say that:
The new forests which are developing in areas which have been harvested or affected by natural disasters are frequently poorer than the forests they are

November 8, 1979
Forestry Research
replacing. They are often inadequate in terms of preferred species, quality, density of stocking, insect and disease resistence or location suitable for economic wood supplies to existing mills.
The expert consensus was that up to 20 per cent of the land harvested every year does not and will not regenerate properly.
Let me remind hon. members that that was said about two years ago.
The communique goes on:
When areas where regeneration was been blighted by insect infestations, fires, and wind damage are added, a total of 647,000 acres is lost from the nation's potentially productive forest stock every year.
This is being added in turn to a backlog of unproductive forest land accumulated over many years which the Canadian Forestry Association estimates at a staggering 60 million acres. Large parts of this wasteland are to be found in every province. In fact, no province can claim that regeneration within its boundaries is even keeping pace with the yearly cut.
Also, according to the association:
Inadequate attention to forest regeneration is responsible for restricting expansion possibilities in some regions, has reduced employment in others, and will result in a continuing decline in future forest based jobs and revenues.
Some experts predict really critical shortages by the end of the century if large scale forest management and renewal programs are not put into effect.
The question therefore arises as to whether or not Canada can catch up. Some of our leading forestry consultants say yes, and I will quote from a report prepared for the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association which states the following:
A more intensive program of forest management is imperative if market opportunities are to be realized and emerging timber deficits offset.
What needs to be done, and we have the know-how and the means, is to develop or apply improved species that grow faster and have more resistance to insects and disease than those seeded naturally. It will take, of course, a deliberate commitment on the part of governments, industry, and indeed the public at large, to ensure that our forests meet our future needs. There are difficult problems of cost, responsibility, ecology and the claims on the forest of industry and recreation which will have to be resolved.
All these elements put together lead to the conclusion that the provinces have demonstrated that they alone cannot achieve this important economic goal as it relates to our forest industries. I submit to the House that Canada needs a national forestry policy. We have evidence, as demonstrated by reports, conferences and statistics which have been published in many quarters, that not only do we need a national forestry policy but we must have such a policy soon, taking into consideration the limitation imposed by our constitution. This policy would offer terrific opportunities.
I would summarize today's problems and opportunities with regard to our forestry industry in this way in submitting the urgency of and the necessity for this policy, which I would like to impress upon members of this government, on the minister responsible and on the government backbenchers who, as we have already seen in the course of this debate in their interventions, feel strongly and positively about this issue.
First, a national forestry policy will have to deal with the deteriorating competitive position of the industry. The industry

needs attention and needs certain incentives. Second, it will offer a challenge and an opportunity to the industry in the provision of adequate forest replacement. Ottawa, in co-operation with the provinces, could launch a program to double the present rate of plantation to 400 million trees a year. This is an investment for future generations of Canadians in the regeneration of our forests to provide for the needs of our consumers and for maintaining our capacity to export this commodity to foreign markets, thus improving our balance of payments.
There is a third aspect which demands enunciation in the launching of a national forest policy, and that is the recent development of the slowing down of the regrowth process which is apparently caused by acid precipitation. This has become a very serious problem which, if not dealt with effectively, could result in the lengthening of the growing cycle of the forest.
Fourth, a national forestry policy would give a coherent approach to the better utilization of wood as a renewable resource, particularly because of the potential it offers to replace fuel. Wood can be used for the production of methanol to replace gasoline. The industry would develop and create jobs in Canada if we were to start a national effort to exploit and use wood for this purpose. This cannot be carried out by an individual province. It is a function that rests squarely on the federal system and on the facilities and resources that the federal government has at its disposal through the National Research Council and other departments.
Another facet of this national forest policy has to do with the environmental impact of forest fires and pests. We are told that over two million acres of forests have been burned over annually for the past ten years. We are also told that insects and other pests damage large tracts of timber each year, the spruce budworm being just one example.
Again, since the causes of these diseases and damage do not really know provincial boundaries, and since the federal government has a fairly sophisticated Department of Agriculture and Department of the Environment, it also has the capacity and the ability to address itself to this particular facet. A national policy, in my view, cannot be developed by ten provinces acting on their own. In the field of forestry we have a classic example where federal leadership is not only needed but is most desirable.
I would, therefore, commend the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), and those who have spoken before me in such positive terms, for having emphasized the importance of this issue and for having given us an opportunity to register with the government the urgency of this matter and the hope that the government will address itself to an announcement in the field of launching for Canadians and for future generations of Canadians a national forestry policy.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON FEASIBILITY OF ESTABLISHING CROWN CORPORATION FOR FORESTRY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate, in the limited amount of time that is left, in this debate on the need for enhancing a
November 8, 1979

national forest policy. In my riding of Sault Ste. Marie there is a federal government forest research centre that is doing splendid work in terms of trying to control the problem of the spruce budworm, as well as research into other areas of interest to our national forests.
In the last Parliament I spoke out very vigorously against announced cutbacks by the former Liberal government in the budget of the forestry service, and pointed out the necessity of enhancing research and development in this vital sector of our economy. To that extent I was supported by my friend, the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), who also argued for enhancement of this important research sector of the federal service. 1 hope he is effective in convincing the Postmaster General and Minister of the Environment (Mr. Fraser) not to proceed with some of these cutback policies initiated by the former government, but to establish a more vigorous profile in the forestry section of the department of the environment in expanding the good work it has been doing.
There have been repeated warnings that we have not been taking the necessary steps to ensure the future of this vital sector of our economy, namely, our nation's forests. Some 12 per cent of our productive forest land is inadequately stocked, and another 500,000 acres are being added to the backlog annually. The plain fact is that neither the federal government, the provincial governments nor private industries concerned are taking the initiatives required in reforestation so that we will have the trees for our lumber and pulp and paper industries in decades ahead. The warning clarion has been sounded, yet 1 fail to see either at the provincial or federal level a recognition that we have a serious problem and that we have to mobilize funds and manpower to redress what is happening to our forests here in Canada.
Indeed, in my part of the country in northern Ontario we are dependent on the forests and, unfortunately, they are not being restocked. The good timberland is being used up too rapidly, and if we do not replenish these valuable renewable resources it will mean a severe, if not disastrous blow to many communities in northern Ontario and, of course, in Quebec and British Columbia as well.
When we look at what has been happening in the forestry service we have to be alarmed. The strength has been cut drastically, by 1,000 man-years since 1968. These are highly qualified scientists and technicians. We have lost them, and as a result many experimental programs in long-range research, so vital to finding solutions to a number of the problems, have not been going on to the degree necessary. Our forest service budget is one quarter of that of the scientific and technological fields of fisheries, energy, mines and resources, or agriculture. I think it is high time the new Conservative government recognized that forestry must have a higher priority, not only in funds but in terms of staff. Indeed, I would argue that a separate ministry of forestry should be established so that this sector of our economy can get the kind of attention it so richly deserves.
In the last Parliament I spoke against the privatization of the forest products laboratories which the Liberal government
Forestry Research
undertook, and which I understand the Conservatives are still following through. This, in my opinion, will not fulfil the goals the government has proposed. We opposed this privatization because we know that the kind of research the private sector carries on is short-term in its outlook. It is quite naturally designed to try to improve the present product situation in terms of new methods of developing and selling products. The private industry does not have the long-term kind of research goals the federal government can have, and this is where we are falling down if we rely on the private sector.
We need more, not less basic research. We need more of an indication from the private sector, which is being subsidized by the taxpayers through all the various forms of government research, that the private sector in turn will reinvest some of its profits in this vital area of research, and that it will really support and do work parallel to that being done by government laboratories.
We need an impartial agency to supply data to foreign powers. I do not think this will be served by private laboratories as there will be a suspicion that the figures are self-serving, particularly because the industry has always performed development work on products and processes, but not the kind of basic research I have described that is so vital to the forestry sector. What we need to find are the technical innovations required to maintain a competitive position, or the Canadian forestry industry will start to deteriorate.
Indeed, we have a morale problem in the Canadian forestry service as a result of the cutbacks initiated last spring. Many of the scientists are moving off to other countries or into the private sector, and those remaining in the federal domain are, as I say, suffering a severe morale problem, wondering to what end is their scientific research.
It seems to me there are four key areas where the federal government must assume some responsibility. We need a continuous statistical survey of resources, and the federal government, looking at the nation as a whole, can carry this out in a way the provinces or private industry cannot. We must have up-to-date information so we can assess the areas where we need to improve forest rehabilitation. We need a program of intensive forest management.
I think we can learn a lot from the Scandinavian countries. For to say, that we have vast acreages of forest in Canada that we need not worry about the future, flies in the face of all the most recent reports that this so-called renewable resource is dwindling. I would like to see a crash program initiated by the federal government, with some kind of financial assistance to the provinces, in order to begin reforestation to the degree that it is necessary. Indeed, we need an industrial strategy-and how often have we heard that word-for long-range planning to make a stable environment for investment in this sector of our economy.
For example, a report prepared by F.L.C. Reed and Associates about a year and a half ago for the federal government points out that although provincial legislation has been in

November 8, 1979
Forestry Research
place for the last 20 to 30 years, forest management is not practised at acceptable levels and Canada lags far behind her major competitors in management of her forest industry. For example, production of seed trees in Ontario nurseries between 1972 and 1976 decreased from 77 million to 51 million, despite increased requirements. We are in an emergency situation and the times demand action.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been through quite an interesting exercise last week and again this week. In my opening remarks I referred to this particular study which was presented to the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers in June. It was from remarks made by the previous minister of the environment that I learned that such a study existed.
1 can only say in these few minutes left to me that I found it quite interesting that the parliamentary secretary and other representatives of the government seemed to get very up tight about the words "Crown corporation" included in the motion. The motion refers to the latest report on the feasibility of establishing-and if we ignore the words "Crown corpora-
November 8, 1979

tion"-some body to carry out forestry research. That is exactly what was being considered-somebody to carry out forestry research in order that a proposal could be made to this meeting of the ministers of the environment in June of this year.
Obviously the need for that was underlined by the parliamentary secretary, when he commented on the fact that in the province of Quebec shortages are occurring, especially for saw logs. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is again a great privilege to speak to the "whole" House this evening. Co-operation and consultation are words we learn about daily from the government benches. But how do the native people feel about this government? Do they feel they are being consulted?
This week the ITC heard about the development of the Arvik mine. They did not hear about it from the minister, or the government, but from the press. In the Yukon, the Council of Yukon Indians heard about the minister granting de facto responsible government on Friday before the announcement was made. That is not consultation. That is not co-operation. It is a fait accompli.
The unilateral decision of the minister of Indian affairs to allow mining and pipeline construction before native land claims are negotiated is pure folly. The government is denying the native people any say on land on which they have lived for generations. These developments will have an adverse effect on the life, the culture and the economic livelihood of the native people. This has certainly been the case elsewhere in Canada.
Last week when the minister refused to ratify the already concluded COPE agreement, it again proved that the government is not interested in the concerns and rights of native people. The assumption by Tories, southern Canadians, and even a few northern Canadians, that responsible government is always just and progressive and will always protect the rights of minorities is just not so. The Manitoba school question and the treatment of the Metis people in Manitoba has proven that this is not the case.
Governments based on cultural identity were accepted before Confederation. For example, the creation of the province of Quebec accepted this very principle. Before that, Upper Canada was created for the United Empire Loyalists. Treaties have always recognized native government and the creation of geographic territories called reserves. Manitoba, in becoming a province, allowed for the ethnic composition of its population. Unfortunately it also demonstrated that the rights of a minority cannot always be left to the goodwill of the majority.
As long as we are talking about the duty of government to protect minorities, why has the federal government continually stalled in selecting an arbitrator for the northern flood agreement? The initial agreement was signed over two years ago. This government and the former Liberal government could have worked faster and harder on this item.
Many questions regarding compensation that northern residents should receive for the flooding of their land cannot be

November 8, 1979

settled and, as usual, it is the natives who suffer. The land is flooded, the fishing affected, and the natives still do not have adequate compensation.
1 understand that the native people and the provincial government have agreed on an arbitrator. It is only the federal government's lack of action that prevents an appointment from being made.
The housing of native people is deplorable and a national disgrace. How does the government expect Indian people to build a house for $12,000? Why does CMHC not provide funds for native people? These are only a few items which these supplementary estimates do not touch. If these estimates dealt with national health and welfare, Mr. Speaker, I would cite a number of examples of neglect and federal-provincial buck passing-and I mean the pun-that are also a mark against this country, and matters that the minister of external affairs would be speaking about in the UN if some other country was perpetrating this disgrace.
The actions of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) have further decreased employment in northern and native communities. The elimination of the Canada Works Program in a number of provinces was both conservative and cruel-the words have become synonymous. The addition of some dollars to the LEAP program did not come close to what Canada Works formerly offered. In my constituency $3.9 million was spent last year on the Canada Works Program. This year there is nothing.

[Mr. Murphy.)
The proof of the success that PetroCan has already demonstrated, and the logic of the Canadian government keeping the last instrument of control it has on the oil industry, and the shameful state of foreign domination of our natural resources, are a result of the past blindness of Liberal and Conservative regimes.

As I look at these supplementary estimates I have trouble telling the difference between Liberal and Conservative governments. I believe that on the matters before us, like on the devastating increases in interest rates, there is no difference between these two old line parties. Both parties sound progressive when in opposition, and conservative when in government. The only difference is that in the choice of a name for their party the Progressive Conservatives are honest; well, at least half honest.
Both parties have forgotten the unemployed, and the small businessmen, especially when it comes to advocating and accepting high interest rates. Both have failed, as is evident in these estimates, to prepare a development plan for northern areas. Instead they have relied on large multinationals and allowed them to create a boom and bust cycle, to ignore the needs of northern residents, to let small business fail when these multinationals desert our northern towns, allowed them to pollute our fish and forests with acid rain, and to fail to employ the indigenous people of northern areas, despite all the promises given when these corporations start up.
If government is to take the reins and provide economic leadership, then it must have a northern development plan, a plan made by northerners within the framework of a national economic strategy, a plan which allows the north to develop its own goals and recognizes the cultural and environmental factors in operation in northern regions, a plan which will help northern residents to benefit from their resources, and a plan which will allow northern residents to become more self-sufficient and to assist in the development of all of Canada.
It is the lack of a northern development plan by the Liberals and the Conservatives that helped in part to have me elected to this House. It has helped to elect a number of other members of my party at the provincial and federal level. In this House there are four members, including myself, who lived in the Churchill constituency during the seventies. They are all New Democrats, and all lived in the riding and saw the effects of Liberal and Conservative neglect. Now they are here to change that.
In conclusion, I would remind the members opposite and the members to my right-before they, like the member from Bow River's dinosaurs, become politically extinct-I remind them that there were 10,000 Manitobans who had to leave their province last year because of the lack of economic planning, the economic devastation that the Lyon Conservative govern-

Mr. Chairman, we have some suggestions for the minister of fisheries, but before we start with those questions-and we will have questions in the hours, days, and weeks ahead here-I want to sketch in some context for those questions.
The context was really begun by the hon. member for Nickel Belt this afternoon when he set the scene in his remarks by indicating the direction in which this government is going. Some people maintain that the government is directionless. That is not true. There appears a certain clear direction and it is the direction of business in this country. We want to show that that direction is being maintained in the fisheries policy as well as elsewhere. Indeed, there is already evidence to show that this is a fact. I am not putting the blame for that policy line at the door of the minister of fisheries. We on this side
November 8, 1979

have a high regard for the minister as an individual, but the government party is now in the hands of the corporate interests represented by Bay Street, and the President of the Treasury Board is becoming known in the Atlantic provinces as "the slasher". I believe the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood had another name for him, but that is the name by which he goes in the Atlantic provinces.
Let me point to some of the evidence for the direction that is taking place in small craft harbours, for example. If that is the government that claims to be on the side of small boat fishermen-which I know the minister of fisheries is-then why was $11 million cut from the small craft harbours' budget this year? We questioned this in the standing committee, and it was quite clear to all of us that $11 million less will be spent on small craft harbours than was going to be spent last year. Those of us from the Atlantic area, not only from this side of the House but also the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte on the other side, will remember the time we spent in the committee on public works improving the small crafts harbours budget, in fact tripling it. The hon. member for Westmorland-Kent, when he was the minister of fisheries, continued the practice that the minister had started before him, and improved it.
This year $11 million less will be spent on small craft harbours. 1 do not know how many members are aware of the importance of this facility in the Atlantic provinces, but there is no point in trying to catch fish if you do not have boats, and you do not have boats if you do not have protection for those boats in the form of wharves and breakwaters, and if you do not have something to pull those boats up on in the wintertime. That is the importance of this to small boat fishermen and that is the importance of it to the Atlantic provinces, but that is the direction this government is taking, and that is the kind of policy line we are getting from this government.
Before I leave the subject of small craft harbours let me say this. Right now the Minister of Employment and Immigration has on his desk waiting for approval certain Canada Works projects in the Atlantic provinces. Whatever other members may think of these particular programs, they have been Godsends for the inshore fishermen in the Atlantic provinces and Quebec. They have had facilities built that would have been built no other way and with no other funds.
Right now ready for approval are Canada Works projects for building wharves, breakwaters, haul-outs, slipways and fishing stages. However, there needs to be complementary money from the small craft harbours budget, and that money is just not there. Those projects will not be approved. In addition to the $11 million of small craft harbours money in the main estimates that will not be spent, these Canada Works funds will be unspent because of the lack of money in the small craft harbours budget. This is a sad situation in the Atlantic area, and I hope I can make clear to the House how serious it is.

The second piece of evidence relates to fishing vessel subsidies. The previous government and, indeed, the present government, have been encouraging small boat fishermen to improve their boats, their catching capability, their technology and their gear, but since June we have not had any fishing vessel subsidies.
A 53-foot longliner in the Atlantic provinces and Quebec costs $500,000. Can you appreciate the difficulty of small boat fishermen, small entrepreneurs, raising that kind of money? The federal government normally pays 35 per cent of the cost of such a vessel, or at least in my province it does. That money has not been there since June. This means that boats that were supposed to have been built have not been built, and this means that fishermen have gone without, in spite of the fact that groundfish are coming back and stocks are being rejuvenated. The fishermen have not got boats with which to prosecute the fishery. This is, indeed, a sad situation.
In addition to that, the shipyards which normally build these vessels and provide additional employment to people in that area have been lying idle. If this is a government of small boat fishermen, where is the small craft harbours money? If this is a government of small boat fishermen, where are the fishing vessel subsidies? They are not available in my province which has the highest unemployment rate in Canada. That province is represented by two ministers in the federal cabinet, and the present premier won his election by saying we had two stars in Ottawa now, and suddenly the heavens were going to open and rain gold. We are still waiting for that gold to rain. Six, seven months have gone by, and still we have not seen the evidence of the work of the two hon. gentlemen in the cabinet. I am not laying this at their doors; 1 am laying it at the doors of the people who are controlling this present party in government at the present time, and back of that party the interests of the large corporate organizations in this country.
The real issue that is developing in the fishery, at least on the Atlantic coast, and I suspect on the Pacific coast as well, is not a conflict between the provinces, and not a conflict between the provinces and the federal government. Richard Cashin, the president of the Newfoundland Fish, Food and Allied Workers Union, in a statement yesterday in Newfoundland defined it very well. He said that the real issue that is developing is not so much a constitutional conflict between the provinces and the federal government or, indeed, between the provinces, but a conflict or a power struggle within the fishing industry, a struggle between the large corporate interests and the small boat fishermen. That is the struggle that is emerging, and that is the struggle we want to address ourselves to on this side.
Let me make it quite clear where we in this party stand, as we have stood before. Whatever the hon. member for Nickel Belt may say about the lack of difference between the parties on both sides of the House in policy, it is quite clear that at least in respect of fisheries the policy of this party has been to favour the disadvantaged, the powerless, the people with the least economic and political powers in the fishing industry, and that has been the fishermen.

November 8, 1979

If there is one thing that the hon. member for Westmorland-Kent was known for it was as the minister of fishermen, not so much as the minister of fisheries.
Hear, hear!

The struggle that is going on within the fishing industry is indeed that struggle between the corporate interests in the fishing industry and the small boat fishermen.
Let me make it quite clear where we stand. We, as a party, want to defend the people whom we have represented over the years and whom we continue to represent in our ridings, and they are the small boat fishermen; the inshore fishermen. We do so not simply because we want to improve their economic position but, indeed, because the small boat or inshore fishermen are tied up in a very integral manner with the way of life in the Atlantic provinces and Quebec. Our communities and our families exist because of the inshore fishery and because of the small boats fishery. We want to protect that way of life, not simply the fishery, and not simply to improve their economic position. That is the issue in the fishery today. The question is: who will get the power and the control, and how will that power be shared among those various sections of the fishery?
I am not going to deal with the issue that has come up most recently, that issue in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. 1 am going to leave that to my friend, the hon. member for Gloucester, who championed that issue from the beginning, assisted by the hon. member for Westmorland-Kent and, indeed, by my colleague, the hon. member for Gaspe. They will deal with that issue in some substance. However, that is further evidence of the direction that is being taken in the interests of the corporate powers within the fishing industry.
The issue of freezer trawlers will be the next important issue we want to debate on this side. We think the minister has been premature in discussing with the Fisheries Council of Canada the issue of freezer trawlers within the fishing industry, because here again a conflict takes place. If we increase the number of licences in the fishery for large vessels with freezing capacity to take large amounts of groundfish, in addition to unutilized species, and there is no way they can be economic unless they take a certain amount of groundfish, and I doubt that they can be economic anyway, that is going to have-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I am sure my friend would not want to mislead the House. I just want to refresh his memory. When the estimates were before the committee I indicated to him that I had not in fact discussed the question of freezer trawlers with the Fisheries Council of Canada.

I accept that from the minister, Mr. Chairman. All we are saying is that before any decision is made we on this side want consultation. We want to be able to debate that whole issue because it is of paramount importance. It is another sub-issue growing out of the one I have been trying to point out. We want to be consulted on that. We want a full debate on it. We want all the facts laid on the table, and we

want adequate consultation with the inshore fishermen whose very livelihood is threatened by this issue of freezer trawlers.
When referring to the struggle between the corporate interests and the small fishermen I would suggest that my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, who is not here today, would raise the issue of the squid fishermen of Chedabucto Bay and the Canso area. It is true that the freezers of the companies are full at the present time. The shame of it is that squid in the areas I have indicated is being thrown overboard because the fishermen cannot get rid of it. The companies say they already have their freezers full and they cannot sell it.
The minister is saying that over-the-side sales will not be approved in this area and that he will not allow foreign vessels to come in and take the squid as they have in the past. If the companies are saying that they do not have a market for thei, squid, will the minister of fisheries speak to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and tell her that there is a dire situation in Cambodia at the present time and we as the government have approved $15 million for that area?
I would remind the minister that the main market for squid which is emerging now is the Japanese market. Would the minister tell the Secretary of State for External Affairs that we have this situation in Chedabucto Bay and Canso, and would he arrange, through whatever means necessary, to ship this product overseas to the people who are in dire need of it at the present time? We in Canada have so much of so many other things. There are people who need that product, and I am sure that something can be worked out in the interest of the squid fishermen in that area so that they can get rid of that product that they are catching and having to throw away at the present time.
I understood the minister to say earlier that he was not against over-the-side sales in principle. I thought I saw in his press release that they probably would continue next year. I hope that the minister will clarify his position on the matter because I think that he has to do something about that situation. It is an important situation for these fishermen in that area and, once again, the people who are affected are the small boat fishermen who cannot get rid of their product. The large corporations are not affected because their freezers are already full with that product.
Another issue which I would like to bring to the attention of the minister of fisheries in the hope that he will pass it on to the Minister of Public Works or possibly the Minister of Transport is the issue of navigational devices on the east coast, and specifically the Loran program. The previous government earmarked $14 million for the installation of new Loran facilities on the Atlantic coast. That has now been put aside, and the project will not go ahead even though all the ground work was laid. The Fox Harbour, Labrador area, was to have a Loran station. It is very important to the fishermen in that area and, indeed, to the U.S. coastguard.
November 8, 1979

I understand that not only are the Canadian fishermen upset, but so is the U.S. coastguard because they cannot navigate in the Atlantic area due to the lack of those Loran facilities. The possibility of oil discoveries off the Atlantic coast is further evidence of the need for these navigational facilities at the present time. Both the present government and the previous government have been encouraging fishermen to get the most up-to-date equipment. That technology will use the Loran navigational equipment for fixes at sea. If the government is encouraging the fishermen to get into that kind of boat and that kind of technology, it must have the proper kind of navigational equipment. It would not make any sense at all to leave that money unspent because one goes hand in hand with the other. I implore the minister to speak to his colleagues, the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Transport, to see if he could have reinstated that $14 million to provide those very necessary Loran facilities on the Atlantic coast.
There are other issues that we would like to raise during the course of this debate. We would like to ask the minister what he intends to do about the Atlantic salmon. He must make a decision on that matter soon. We now know that the stock is in a great deal of trouble and that the decision will not be easy. There are five or six different factors, and during the course of the debate we will be going into this matter in more detail. 1 hope that the decision on that matter will be in the interest of those who need that salmon most and, again, in our opinion that is the small boat fishermen.
One option open to the minister is to reduce or possibly eliminate the salmon catch at the present time in Newfoundland. Certainly, the policy taken by the government of New Brunswick would suggest that it has not brought the stocks back, and I doubt very much if implementing that kind of policy with regard to Newfoundland would make any more sense. 1 think that there are other ways and means to go about solving the salmon problem.
The difficulty we on this side see is the direction in which we are heading in fisheries policy. It is a clear departure from the policy followed by the previous minister of fisheries. If the hon. member for Nickel Belt is looking for a difference in philosophy or approach, then let him look at the fishery policy because, from our point of view, there is a clear difference which we do not like and which we would like to see changed.

Mr. Chairman, as I understand it we are on Schedule A at the present time. The hon. member directed his comments I think to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, which is referred to in schedule D. For purposes of good order, 1 would suggest that each speaker deal with the schedule before us, and in that way we can proceed in a more orderly way with any questions that may be raised. The reason I say this is because schedule A is really where my hon. friend's points are going to come up on the twelve-twelfths. Schedule A deals with the three-twelfths that we are asking for in addition to the usual nine-twelfths that are dealt with in the bill.
Schedule B deals with the request for two-twelfths, the final schedule is the request for one-twelfth, and schedule D deals

with the supplementary estimates A. It is supplementary estimates A that have the provision with respect to fisheries and oceans. I could suggest that we come to the various fisheries and oceans discussion points either in schedule D, or when we revert to some of the clauses which we have stood. For example, clause 2(a) is the general nine-twelfths provision which includes, of course, fisheries and all the other departments. I am suggesting that perhaps if we could deal with schedule A we could get that behind us and then schedules B and C, and hopefully we could get to schedule D quickly.

In view of the fact that we agreed with the government House leader that we would be discussing the fisheries estimates, we were prepared to go to that on clause 2. We stood the other clauses in order to be co-operative. In view of that, would it not be acceptable to the President of the Treasury Board, and to you Mr. Chairman, if we stood schedules A, B and C and went to schedule D, because we are prepared to discuss it?
We thought that we would be dealing with clause 2 and that we could do everything on that clause. That is why we would rather stand the others and go to schedule D. Would that be acceptable?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have no objection. I had the same preoccupation as the President of the Treasury Board, but by stretching schedule A with regard to marine transportation, I found a way to accept the remarks of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, although at times he referred more to fisheries than to wharfs and shipbuilding. I have no objection to that, but to stand schedules A, B, C, and go to D, would need the consent of the committee.

From the point of view of this party, Mr. Chairman, we are not prepared to stand this clause at the moment. We still have a number of speakers on it and I think we need its generalities in order to bring up things that are of great concern to those members who are present tonight and who will be present tomorrow, immediately after question period.

Mr. Chairman, I am not sure if the hon. member who just spoke was here when his House leader agreed to stand clause 2. We have prepared ourselves to discuss clause 2. If they want to discuss something else, we have no objection to the Chair recognizing them proportionately, for the evening. I think it is unfair of the hon. member to bring this up now, when we have agreed to his leader's suggestion to stand clause 2. We are not saying they cannot discuss whatever they want to discuss, if they want an equitable share of the time for debate, but it is very unfair of the member from the New Democratic Party to refuse us the opportunity to discuss what we want to discuss.
We have no objection, Mr. Chairman, if you recognize them equitably this evening-as you always do, of course-but 1

wish the hon. member would not refuse consent for us to discuss what we want to discuss. We were ready to go ahead on clause 2. Mr. Chairman, it is true I was out of the House so I do not want to contradict any commitment made earlier that we would prefer to stay with schedule A, standing the various clauses. That is what I heard when I came into the House. I am not aware that we have any objection to that, as long as we stay with schedule A.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me there is really no problem. If we accept the advice you gave the committee in the first place, we can talk about fisheries under the marine transportation program and we can ask the questions that we want to as well.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The committee will have to decide for itself. Right now I am faced with a decision that has been made to stand clauses 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. We are on schedule A now. If hon. members cannot agree among themselves, we will have to proceed with schedule A and I shall try to keep the debate as orderly as I can.
Shall schedule A carry?

Mr. Chairman, if I understood your last remark it means there will be a fairly free-ranging discussion. That is probably the way most hon. members would like it.

This is a new experience for quite a few of us and I suspect the wise and learned views of some of our colleagues would have been useful in the last few minutes. However, we shall muddle through.
Any discussion on fisheries must take place in a rather bizarre context for those of us who remember the period of 1974-75. Most of the tensions and the debate taking place in regard to fisheries matters at the moment are caused by a problem of riches. There is an abundance of fish. It is because the fishery has become so attractive to so many that a lot of discussion is taking place. I modestly take some slight credit for this abundance of riches, although I suspect the oceans are mainly responsible for creating the biological wealth. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans now finds himself approached on many sides by those who want to get in on the action.
The first time we took issue with him was on the decision to allow the larger vessels back into the Gulf of St. Lawrence which came about as a result of conflicting fishermen's interest groups competing for the same fish. The hon. member for Gloucester will have more to say on this issue a little later. I suspect a whole series of issues of the same nature are pending. Reference was made to freezer trawlers. If these vessels are to receive additional licences and not replacements, we will want to know who is to get that next generation of licences. If it is those who can afford them because they already have large fleets, then we will want to know the criteria under which the licences were issued.
We will also want to know if the minister has abandoned the policy enunciated in 1977, to the effect that the holders of fishing licences should not also be the processors or marketers of fish, that there will be a separation of the fleet to create a clientele, if I can use that word, of fishermen who own their boats individually or collectively and who go into the business of fishing while others go into the business of processing and marketing.
When I held that portfolio I concluded that the system whereby large trawlers could transfer some cost other than the cost of catching the fish, created unfair competition for a lot of small boat owners.
In any discussion about the next generation of licences, 1 would be interested in hearing the minister's views on an idea which 1 suggested and which the Premier of Newfoundland espoused at an open federal-provincial conference. It was a matter of public record that the idea of the next generation of licences, or the increase in the licences, should not be in the hands of those who already have them, but should be distributed or put in the hands of a consortium. This consortium could be comprised of a company in which government, present processors possibly, and fishermen, would be represented and in which they would have a say. Fishermen will certainly want to have something to say about the allocation of what I call the next generation of licences.
November 8, 1979

There are a number of other areas in which the sources of conflict between competing groups, not only fishermen but of processors and fishermen, are coming to the fore. Look at the situation on the sale of squid. It is possible that that market has slowed down. Have the companies, before asking the minister to intervene on their behalf, made available to fishermen through their organization all information which would allow fishermen to make a reasonable judgment? The fishermen of British Columbia in the herring roe know the market can bear roughly 90 thousand tons. Way beyond that figure market conditions and their income as fishermen would be in danger. This knowledge is shared among companies and fishermen and they arrive at a reasonable decision.
Those companies which were at my door when I was minister and must be at my successor's door in order to get access to the offshore squid have created very little employment. Squid was caught by freezer trawlers. These ships were chartered. The squid was then transferred to carrier or reefer vessels and taken to the Japanese market. Those companies at that time were not overly worried about the glut condition of the market.
I suspect that having their freezers full and having served themselves very nicely, thank you, then the fishermen who would like to sell fish to Japanese freezers in bays like St. George's Bay-the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion knows very well what I am talking about-find themselves prohibited by this minister whose instincts I am sure are repelled by having to make this sort of decision.
The minister will have to learn one thing, that he will have to resist a popularity contest with the large processors in the fishing industry who have traditionally exercised pressure and who have resisted some of the policies I advocated to allow fishermen to come home as equal partners. He will have to resist the blandishments of those who spoke yesterday to the committee that one had to exploit the fish on what one had to call an economic basis, that is, the fastest buck for the fewest possible. Then things are closed down and the government is left to worry about the rest.
Obviously this is a resource which belongs to the people of Canada and in which there has been almost no investment by large processors. The only investment has been in vessels acquired, accompanied by good tax write-offs, to capture the fish.
A Liberal write-off.
If the hon. member to my left listened, he might learn a few things.
Like the difference between cod and herring.

The principle of saying to fishermen that when companies do not like it, one must not be allowed to sell fish directly to a foreign freezer, is one that will be hotly debated. We cannot hold the fishermen of this country as hostages to the sort of rhetoric we heard this week in the

House of Commons Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
If the minister wants to be on the side of the fishermen he will have to take his lumps from those who can advertise in The Globe and Mail-
At the taxpayers' expense.

Yes, at the taxpayers' expense, because obviously this is written off. These are the people who were so poor a few years ago that at one point they asked me to take over the fleet. They were telling me they could not afford to run it any more. Now that the government has bailed them out with millions and millions of taxpayers' dollars, they are right back to where they were a few years ago.
They are not interested in long term policies like market consolidation for the foreign market effort of Canada. They are not very much interested in developing new markets as long as they can make a fast overnight dollar in some quick chartering operation. The minister will have to come down on one side or the other. I hope that he is brave enough to resist these ideological neo-conservatives who are developing some new altars on which we are supposed to sacrifice in the next few years. As the minister from Nova Scotia said, the fishermen of Cape Breton have been suckered in when trying to defend their interests as small inshore fishermen.
The minister will have to decide if he will speak on behalf of the fishermen or if he will speak on behalf of those he called good corporate citizens the other day. I suspect at some point he will not be able to speak comfortably for both.
I had intended to say a few more words, but I will conclude by saying that I think fishermen's organizations must not be prohibited, as they are in certain provinces, where by law fishermen do not have the right to organize-I am embarrassed to say that my own province of New Brunswick is one of those-
Under a Tory government.

Yes, under a Conservative government. The fishermen of this country must be given a chance to defend their interests as every other group of society is allowed to do. Not only that, but they must be actively encouraged by being heard and listened to. I intend to speak on some other items, but for the moment those are my general remarks.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to talk about fish.
Do you know what cod is?

I want to ask a particular question of the President of the Treasury Board. It will take only three minutes and it arises from discussions 1 have had today. Can he tell us whether it is the intention of the government to announce before Christmas further sales of additional Crown corporations?

Mr. Chairman, I am not sure whether or not that comes under schedule A but I will answer the hon.

November 8, 1979
Supply
member in this way: it is likely that the privatization candidate list with respect to Crown corporations will be increased, and an announcement will be made sometime between now and Christmas.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is here in committee. In the last few weeks there have been many subjects that we have wanted to raise with him and he has been good enough to make himself available in the committee on fisheries and forestry. We appreciate that.
I want to say, as have my friends, the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, and the hon. member for Westmorland-Kent, that it is nice to see the Minister of Fisheries sitting with the President of the Treasury Board. One could not exemplify better the problems that are happening with fisheries now. Because this is the start of the session, we want to be nice; we are not going to be difficult right away. As I have said many times in this House to the hon. member for St. John's East, we hope he will be able to do those things that he wants to do.
I wish the President of the Treasury Board would forget his ideology and his blanket cutbacks and slashing on discretionary spending, and realize that what he is doing is humiliating all his colleagues whose departments have, as a vocation, spending and development. After four or five months I do not understand how the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans can sit at the same desk as the President of the Treasury Board, considering the difficulties he has caused. I do not understand how the minister can go back to Newfoundland and the rest of the Atlantic provinces to give an explanation to the fishermen, town councils, village councils, chambers of commerce and all kinds of industrial companies. You know what I am talking about, Mr. Chairman. It must be extremely difficult for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to explain why, for philosophical reasons, changes were made on a certain date, June 1.
I want to take this opportunity to say what a good job was done by the former minister of fisheries and oceans. Everyone in the Atlantic provinces who knows anything about fisheries agrees with that. Yesterday or the day before in the regional development committee none other than the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans was saying how prosperous rural Newfoundland had become. He stated how economic activity in rural Newfoundland and in fact all over the Atlantic provinces was really alive. That is only because the former minister had influence on the government, something we hope this minister will have before too long.
As I said, we will be nice for a while and give him the benefit of the doubt. The previous minister had influence in the government because our party thought that fisheries was important. That is because external affairs and the diplomatic infrastructure of this country pushed at the Law of the Sea Conference to get the 200-mile limit settled. I was present at many discussions where the former minister pushed the government into unilaterally declaring the 200-mile limit.

It was not only because of the 200-mile limit the fisheries began to prosper. It was because we had a minister, a government and a party which believed we should put our money where our mouth was. That was what we did.
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador stated that the budget for small craft harbours last year was about $41 million on a yearly basis. It is now being cut to something like $32 million. That is shameful. We have lost a building season in small craft harbours.
This is the first time in 20 years in my constituency that the traditional construction companies had to lay off men in the month of July. I cannot speak for all of New Brunswick, but I know that in northern New Brunswick, which encompasses three constituencies, not one contract has been signed by the Department of Public Works for any marine structure for fisheries paid for under the small craft harbours program since June 4. That is shameful.
The fishery is an important sector. It is important to the culture and the life of our communities. For a government to accept a fiscal policy to freeze discretionary spending is not only humiliating for members like the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans but it is a policy that does not make any sense. In the past three or four months I have met with fishermen and development associations. They cannot believe the Government of Canada wants to follow a policy of freezing discretionary spending for small craft harbours.
My friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador mentioned that the Canada Works program brought in by the Liberal government was a good program. We have worked with officials and community organizations in our constituencies with regard to making as much use as possible of this program to repair wharves and build small structures, something that can be done by those in the communities. This too was initiated by the hon. member for Westmorland-Kent while minister of fisheries. He convinced Treasury Board and the bureaucracy that it would not only provide employment for fishermen but would be more economical and efficient. As my friend said, hundreds of thousands of dollars had been approved under Canada Works.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and his officials will have to tell the community organizations that they are sorry, they have no money. That is shameful. I wanted to emphasize what was said by the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, because the President of the Treasury Board is in the chamber.
I wish to discuss a subject that I am sure we will have ample time to discuss with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans in the days before this bill is approved. On August 22 the minister announced a decision to increase the quotas for cod in regions 4T and 40 in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. He also announced he would provide 6,000 metric tons off that quota to fishing vessels, trawlers 100 feet or more. He permitted them to come back to region 4T of the Gulf of St. Lawrence for the first time since 1975, at which time they had been asked by the then minister, the hon. member for Westmor-
November 8, 1979

land-Kent, not to do so. I spoke to the minister since that time. We raised the matter in the House.
[ Translation]
The minister has been told, I do not know how many times, that if he really made a mistake, we would understand that: it is quite possible for a man who has been a minister for only about ten weeks to make an error; there is so much material to be gone over and assimilated in so short a time that a mistake would be understandable; but, Mr. Chairman, what this minister did was to make an irresponsible decision. He decided to allow trawlers of 100 feet or more to enter the 4T zone in the Gulf of St. Lawrence without consulting anyone but the owners of those trawlers. The minister has replied several times in the House, and I have a few answers here in my hand which 1 would like to quote because I think that the minister, though he may not want to mislead the House deliberately is trying to be "tortuous". And just in case someone does not understand what I mean by that, 1 want to say that-

-the minister has been devious.

Mr. Chairman, on October 17, in reply to my colleague from Gaspe the minister said, and I quote:

Mr. Speaker, that decision was taken after scientific advice had come to us-

The quotation can be found on page 296 of Hansard for October 17.

-that we could take an additional 13,000 metric tons in the Gulf. On the basis of that advice, consultations were held with the Atlantic Groundfish Advisory Committee. There was consultation, and on the basis of that consultation it was agreed that 4,000 metric tons would be assigned the Gulf-based vessels, which left an additional 9,000 metric tons. We decided-
When he answers he is very clever. He just spoke about consultations on the increase of the quota.
We decided that on the basis of that new TAC, we would assign 6,000 metric tons to the 100-footers, or the offshore fleet which had fished in the Gulf prior to 1976.
Again, yesterday, in the House of Commons the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Prime Minister, in answer to a question from the hon. member for Gaspe, said there had been consultations on the question of the entry of the 100-footers. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans should come clean with the House and tell us if he did consult with the governments of New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, Quebec and Nova Scotia on the question of entrance into the Gulf of St. Lawrence in region 4T of these large trawlers. subtopic: HOUSING-REQUEST CANADIAN HOME INSULATION PROGRAM BE EXTENDED
HOUSING-REQUEST CANADIAN HOME INSULATION PROGRAM BE EXTENDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 7 last I put a question either addressed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) or, as it turns out, the minister in charge of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, with respect to the home insulation program. The program has laudable objectives. The main objective, of course, is to encourage people who own private homes to insulate them and therefore reduce the amount of energy they are consuming in order to heat their homes.
Originally the program provided financial assistance to those people who owned homes erected prior to 1946. In the middle of the last federal election, on April 20, the then minister of energy, mines and resources all of a sudden came out with a new plan. He extended the program to homes built prior to 1961 and arranged for people to obtain up to $500, a real scoop, in order to assist them in their home insulation.
What concerns many of my constituents is that the standards of home insulation for houses built during the 1950s and 1960s, indeed until the early 1970s when our energy problems became apparent, were virtually the same. The same type of standard of insulation was required in my municipality and, I suspect, in most municipalities across Canada. Yet the program was extended to provide for assistance to those persons who own homes that were built prior to 1961.
There are people in my constituency who live on the same street, and some of them have houses built prior to 1961 or in 1961. In both cases the houses are virtually the same in terms of design and insulation, yet what this package does is to make fish of some people and fowl of others.
Second, there are a great number of people in subdivisions who, being good and intelligent citizens of Canada, insulated their homes prior to April of this year. Some of them have written to me complaining bitterly that they paid for their insulation with their money and now it is their taxes that are being used to help their neighbours insulate.
It is not a question of a program to assist the poor. This is not a program to assist the deprived in our society. It is a program to assist home owners, a program to assist only certain home owners who happen to own houses built prior to 1961. It is not a program that is designed to conserve fuel oil. Indeed, that is the major energy resource of which we are short. We have lots of electricity, presumably we have lots of natural gas because we are exporting more of it, and we have

lots of coal. Indeed, we have a surplus on the energy account of over $1,008 billion in trade. What we are short of is petroleum.
The program does not differentiate between electrically heated homes, oil heated homes, gas heated homes, or wood heated homes for that matter. It is a program that gives certain people for undisclosed reasons the benefit and the right of going to the treasury and saying, "Give me 500 bucks, please;" a program that says to others that they can pay the taxes to cover its cost.
I have raised the issue with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, though I must admit I have not raised it with the minister who is struck with administering the program, that is, the minister in charge of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The matter has been brought home forcefully in the committee where the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie), in talking about the fiscal problems of Canada, has said that the program is costing a fortune and we do not know what the end to it will be. In looking at Supplementary Estimates (B) I see that there is another $120 million for this program in addition to the original $47,300,000 in Estimates (A). I am told, in talking with people more familiar with how to read these estimates, that buried somewhere else is another $15 million or $20 million, and the amount goes up and up. Where are we going, and why should some people get this and some people not?
