subtopic: INTERNATIONAL TRADE-MEASURES TO PROMOTE CANADIAN EXPORTS
INTERNATIONAL TRADE-MEASURES TO PROMOTE CANADIAN EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in addressing a question to the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Wilson) on October 24, 1 had in mind the fact that governments today are everywhere more active in promoting exports. This is hardly surprising in a world where reduced tariff and non-tariff barriers offer additional opportunities. Canada is more dependent than most nations upon trade for its prosperity, and being outside the great trading blocs will feel this competition all the more.
In the past, our search for additional markets has been global. However, the combined impact of geography and investment has ensured that almost three quarters of our trade-much of which is in fact inter-company transfers-is today with one country, the United States. This involves additional constraints on our export opportunities. On two occasions recently the Minister of State has deplored the limitations placed by parent companies on the exports of certain foreign-controlled subsidiaries in Canada. The minister has, however, said nothing yet of what he intends to do.
With further reference to the United States, the minister announced some months ago that Canada's search for new overseas markets has failed. He urges that we must now concentrate on the United States. I would in turn urge the minister not to give up so easily. Both patience and determination are essential to develop new markets. Canadian initiatives in Europe, Japan and the Third World need not imply any slackening of our efforts to sell in the United States. We can do several things at once-and do them all well-if we but have the determination to do so.
In addition to the constraints on Canadian exports resulting from the high degree of foreign investment, another arises from a variety of barriers to internal trade. To achieve an
Adjournment Debate
internationally competitive industry generally requires a domestic launching pad. Various provincial purchasing, labour and investment policies are a self-inflicted handicap in creating such a domestic base, as well as contributing to inflation. What measures does the government intend to take to reduce or eliminate such barriers to industrial rationalization for the enhancement, inter alia, of our export capacity? While on the subject of federal-provincial relations, what does the government intend to do to encourage the elimination of the wasteful duplication in export promotion between the two levels of government?
My comment on our self-imposed barriers to trade within Canada leads to an observation about the continuing absence of an industrial strategy, a strategy that must focus on sectors, including their export potential, and provide a greater degree of consultation and planning among business, labour, and the federal and provincial governments. Without such a strategy much of the work of FIR A and the Canada Development Corporation must necessarily continue in a sort of vacuum. And so must some of our export promotion activities.
1 hope that in replying, the minister will not merely refer to the national economic conference which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. de Cotret) is reported to be planning. We do not need another conference to recognize that yet further improvement in formal consultation and planning among the major players in our economy has become a pressing necessity.
One more point about the need to relate export promotion to an industrial strategy is that, as a result of recent GATT agreements, we shall in eight years reach virtual free trade with the United States. If we fail in the time ahead to increase Canadian control of our own industries, and their ability to compete abroad, I am not confident that we shall be able to retain our remaining economic independence in what will virtually be a free market between Canada and the United States.
In raising a few fundamental questions about export promotion, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to overlook the shorter term techniques. In a recent speech, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce urged the private sector to do more for themselves in seeking export markets. The Canadian Press reported that the minister subsequently added, and I quote, that "government intervention on their behalf has ended . . . including market surveys and trade negotiations".
Is this a statement of new government policy, or has the minister been misquoted? Apparently, in way of explanation, the Minister of State for International Trade said in this House on October 24, as reported at page 549 of Hansard:
There is no intention on the part of this government to remove itself from assistance on trade promotion or trade negotiations where it is appropriate for the government to be involved.
Does this mean that certain past trade promotion practices are now considered by the government to be inappropriate public sector activities? If so, what specific public sector

November 8, 1979
Adjournment Debate
activities does the government hope that the private sector will now assume? There is no point in the government lecturing the business community on their alleged shortcomings when the government itself does little more than confuse the observer about its intentions.
Does the government, in fact, intend to reduce or eliminate market surveys, as has been reported, at a time when the Canadian Export Association has made clear its dissatisfaction with both the quality and distribution of market intelligence? If the government does not intend to continue to engage in trade negotiations and somehow to leave these to the private sector, does it mean all trade negotiations or only certain ones? If so, which ones? Any withdrawal would seem especially paradoxical when the government itself forecasts a record trade deficit.
Against this background, how does the government intend to provide Canadian exporters with services equivalent to those available to our competitors? Let me cite two areas of concern. In export financing, Canadian exporters face disadvantages in competing with Europe and the United States.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Etobicoke North (Mr. McLaren) has raised questions of fundamental interest, and it is a pleasure for me to represent my colleague, the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Wilson), this evening in order to respond to him.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has in place a series of export support programs and marketing services which have an excellent success record and have wide support in the export community.
The trade commissioner service, which has been in existence for over 80 years, enjoys a reputation as one of the world's finest overseas trade promotion organizations. This organization is the main focal point for the preparation of market surveys, to which the hon. member referred, and the question of information on trade opportunities abroad. Their efforts are supported in Ottawa by a number of sectoral and geographical specialists who provide marketing expertise as well as advising direction on trade negotiations.
Among the direct marketing programs administered by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is our program for export market development or, as it is known, PEMD. This program has been increasingly utilized by the exporting community. For example, there has been a 60 per cent increase in appplications for PEMD assistance in the last year.
I would also point out the current government initiative known as Export Canada "79". This is a $1.6 million initiative, aimed at assisting small and medium size manufacturers and processors, many of whom are new in export business.
In the area of overseas trade missions and trade fairs, I would point out that spending for 1979-80 for the promotional
[Mr. MacLaren.)
project program will be over $7 million and increased for $5 million in 1978-79.
The importance of export promotion is further underscored by the government's initiative in creating the cabinet position of Minister of State for International Trade. For the first time in history there is a minister whose principle mandate is to promote international trade. This appointment has again been most welcomed by the business community and, more specifically, the export business community.
While several of the aforementioned programs have been in existence for several years, the government is currently undertaking a review, under the direction of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, with a view to making these programs more accessible to Canadian firms, more streamlined, and more cost-effective.
This review will include the final report of the private sector task force, which is examining the export promotion apparatus. This task force is studying how government can most effectively and efficiently support the private sector in its effort to sell Canadian goods and services abroad.
It is certainly not the intention of this government to simply maintain the status quo but rather to expand these programs so as to capitalize more fully on the efforts of the Canadian exporters.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-ELECTION CAMPAIGN PLATFORM OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-ELECTION CAMPAIGN PLATFORM OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my questions were raised on October 30 and November 2 with regard to an attempt on my part and on the part of my colleagues to uncover the validity of the government's favourite response to every question that has been posed by the opposition regarding economic issues, a response that indicates that no action is now possible and that the election promises made by the "now" government cannot be kept due to the terrible state of the economy left by the previous government.
My question was intended at that time, to show what I believe to be the facts, that the current government knew full well the state of the economy, and in spite of that knowledge made promises to the people of Canada that could not be kept after the campaign. They knew full well at the time that these promises could not be kept without creating economic chaos.
What response was provided to me? The response was precisely the same response that we had received for the previous four weeks. We were told that no action was possible due to some hidden factors that were only discovered by this government after taking office. We asked on another occasion in the same vein to specify in which area these hidden factors were to be found. Were they to be found in inflation? Were they to be found in economic growth? Were they to be found in the current account deficit, in investment, or in savings? Where were these hidden factors to be found? We have not to this day received even a semi-adequate response to any of these questions of an economic nature.
November 8, 1979

Mr. Speaker, the responses we have been getting in this House with regard to economic issues are pure and utter rubbish. Contrary to what people were led to believe, this government has no concrete policies in the area of economics. This government has wasted its years in opposition, years that an opposition should be using for reflection and policy formulation. This government wasted its time with vacuous criticism and the creation of what it knew at the time to be unrealistic promises.
I am certain that this government had clear knowledge of reality during those months prior to the election campaign. The evidence is there. The facts are well documented from comments made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie), and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens). These can be found in Hansard, and in the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and other committees of an economic nature. The questions that were asked and responses given in the House and in the committees indicated quite clearly that the government of this day knew full well what the economic situation was that they were getting into prior to the election. But they were more concerned with destroying the government than with developing policy alternatives. The result is what we see now: six months of inaction, six months of ad hockery, with no sign of well thought out priorities.
This government made promises during the campaign which they had no intention of keeping, no intention whatsoever. Let me cite examples. First, the embassy move. This was a clear case of crass political opportunism, one that has and will continue to cost Canada dearly. Second, the mortgage and property tax credit bill is another example. This is a costly, unaffordable, inequitable, ineffective and unnecessary election goody which the Minister of Finance admits is a millstone around his financial neck. This is crass political gimmickry of the worst sort and people are beginning to see the light.
The government says it has no options with regard to monetary and fiscal policy. That is nonsense, Mr. Speaker. There are options. The problem is, and it is becoming clearer each day, that this government does not understand the nature of the problems we face. It has not considered the alternatives and it has not produced any new thoughts in this area.
This is a time for new initiatives. Instead of new initiatives, we are getting a stall game. The government has no new ideas for restructuring the ailing Canadian economy. It never did, and 1 contend that it is defrauding the Canadian public. The stall game will not work much longer. People are getting wise. 1 have heard it said in my riding and in my travels throughout Ontario that people are beginning to realize that this government is on the ropes. It is bankrupt. It is bankrupt, not financially, but intellectually and morally. The members of the government know that I am right.
We already hear of rifts in the Tory ranks, rifts which indicate that they never were firm on any major new policy directions before the election and are now frantically trying to find a consensus. Members on the other side are in for a rude awakening. The public is starting to demand action and
Adjournment Debate
answers. From what we have been hearing over the past few weeks, this government is going to be hard put to deliver either.

I will try to confine my response to the question the hon. member asked and not to the other references he made. The question related to financial surprises that this government encountered after taking office on May 22. I would like to recite four or five examples of such surprises that we encountered.
First, the Liberal regime had never publicly forecast federal revenues, expenditures and the deficit more than 18 months in advance. On July 20, 1979, however, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) released to the public four-year forecasts to fiscal 1983 that had been prepared during the previous administration. What we discovered was most astonishing.
These forecasts showed a steadily increasing budgetary deficit from $11.8 billion in fiscal 1980 to $14 billion in fiscal 1983, and a doubling of the federal net debt from $51.5 billion in fiscal 1979 to $104.7 billion in fiscal 1983. The forecasts were in sharp contrast to the Liberal claim last year that the federal deficit problem was a temporary phenomenon.
Second, in his last budget the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien), had spoken of a "sustained expansion" of the Canadian economy. According to the former minister, the expansionary forces already at work suggested that he should not stimulate the economy further. The new government found the U.S. and Canadian economies sliding toward recession. The official forecast on which the former minister's fiscal policy was based was wrong and known to be wrong by that government. Less than three months after it had been made, the former minister was already making changes to it.
Third, and most important, when it looked at the assets and debt of Canada, the new government discovered that the accounts of Canada did not properly represent the financial position of this country. In the Accounts of Canada Adjustment Act, the government proposed to write off more than $3.9 billion of assets, the carrying value of which was questionable. While the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Andras) was quite correct in noting that such adjustments do not affect the cash requirement, such adjustments increase the net debt of Canada by the amount of the write-off, almost $4 billion.
Further distortions were found in the treatment of some Crown corporation borrowing. Such borrowing, which exceeded $1.15 billion in fiscal 1979, does not appear in the accounts of Canada.
